#4801. You Can See Everything on the Surface, Not What Lies Beneath

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

I’m writing from the Hamptons. It’s the off-season, and the place feels like a small town, albeit a small town full of influential people, big thinkers, and, yes, some big egos. Almost everyone here is talking about You Can See Everything.

“Do you believe her? Aren’t her eyes crazy? Is she a narcissist? And what about her partner? Was he the real villain?”

It’s human nature to sort people into categories. We want to figure out what happened, so we won’t get fooled ourselves. We want a villain and a victim. We also want to feel better about ourselves, because at least we’re not “that crazy.” And it makes good theater.

If you haven’t seen the film: In the 34 days before Elizabeth Holmes reported to federal prison, she and her partner, Billy Evans, let a film crew led by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim record nearly every move. On the surface, the goal seemed to be showing them as everyday parents: raising their kids, walking on the beach, making eggs.

The title makes a promise: full access, nothing hidden, the real person behind the headlines at last.

The movie is disorienting. It took me a while to process. I won’t share all my thoughts here, but one has stayed with me: A camera can see everything on the surface. It can’t see the hidden drivers underneath.

A camera records behavior: what we say, how we stand, the stories we tell. It rarely captures the why. Under every polished performance and every bad decision, a hidden driver is steering. Unless you’re looking for it, you’ll miss it.

In my work as an executive coach, I use an assessment that uncovers these drivers and lays out the good, the bad, and the ugly in each one. I didn’t create it, and to be clear, it isn’t a personality test. It measures drive: the deep needs that push us forward.

I’ve never assessed Elizabeth Holmes, and I won’t guess at what drives her. But I have coached many founders and tech leaders, and her story reminds me of one of them. She happens to be a woman, but many men fall into the same trap. Her story shows what happens when hidden drivers go unseen.

From a distance, Laura had it all. She was brilliant, fast-moving, and, on paper, wildly successful. She carried herself as if she were the only one in the know and everyone else was slow to catch up.

When you asked her a question, she didn’t answer it. She used the moment to show how much more she knew. I could see why the people around her stopped asking questions. Nobody wants to feel stupid.

Her assessment results explained why. They showed two strong hidden drivers.

The first was going it alone. Somewhere in childhood, Laura’s brain had learned a rule: I can only count on myself. Needing anyone makes me weak.

The second was winning. Second place was not an option.

Put the two together, and her behavior makes sense. Being the smartest person in the room kept Laura in charge. If she always knew better, she never had to need anyone. And every conversation became a contest she could win.

As executive coach Marshall Goldsmith puts it, “Half the leaders I have met don’t need to learn what to do. They need to learn what to stop.”

Laura had built a life where she never had to need anyone. The cost was that no one could truly reach her: not her team, not even her best friend.

I see this pairing of drivers in high-performing leaders all the time. In many ways, it’s what got them to the top. But every driver has a shadow side.

People driven to go it alone tend to keep information to themselves, especially information that makes them look bad. People driven to win have trouble knowing a battle worth fighting from one that’s costing everyone around them.

I sat down with Laura and gently walked her through her results. I told her what her drivers were giving her and what they might cost her.

She listened. Then she said, “I’d like to take the test again.”

I told her the truth: It doesn’t work that way. A hidden driver isn’t a mood that changes depending on how you slept. It’s more like the foundation of a house. You can repaint the walls and rearrange the furniture, but the foundation stays where it was poured.

Here’s what I didn’t say out loud: Her request for a re-test was her drivers at work. To someone driven to go it alone, feedback sounds like “You need help.” To someone driven to win, a hard result feels like losing. So, she did what her drivers had always taught her to do. She tried to beat the test instead of learning from it.

That moment was a choice point: a small gap between what happened and what she did next. In that gap, Laura could have gotten curious. Instead, she reverted to the comfort of her drivers on autopilot.

A few years later, I heard that Laura had lost everything due to her own pride and arrogance: her company, her investors, her own money, and her reputation. I wasn’t surprised. Without awareness, there’s no way to change. Left unchecked, any of us can sabotage ourselves.

I’ve worked with other leaders who share Laura’s drivers and did change. They learned to reflect on themselves and take responsibility for their behavior. Laura never did.

Patterns begin in childhood. Attachment researchers have studied Laura’s pattern for decades. John Bowlby, the father of attachment theory, described people who become “compulsively self-reliant.” Adults with this pattern tend to hide or play down their feelings so they won’t look vulnerable, weak, or dependent on others.

Think of it like this: A child who learns that needing people isn’t safe builds a suit of armor. The armor protects the child. But decades later, the adult is still wearing it and wonders why no one can get close.

Fear makes everyone go quiet. Laura’s need to look smart came with a hidden price. Research on harsh bosses has found that abusive supervision makes employees afraid, and fear leads them to go silent. Harvard’s Amy Edmondson, who studies what she calls psychological safety, found that when it was missing, people were less willing to speak up, ask for help, or admit mistakes, so teams learned less.

Bad news stops traveling upward. Psychologists call this the “Mum Effect.” People tend to soften or hold back bad news, especially when it must go to someone powerful. Stanford professor Robert Sutton described a chilling example. After the 1986 Challenger disaster, physicist Richard Feynman found that NASA’s working engineers put the chance of losing a shuttle at roughly 1 in 100. NASA’s managers put it at 1 in 100,000. The truth had been softened at every step on its way up.

Now put the pieces together. Laura hid her own bad news about her failing company because her self-reliance wouldn’t let her look weak. Her team hid their bad news because she made them feel stupid for speaking up. She ended up leading from inside a bubble where nobody told her the truth, not even herself.

Her drivers weren’t what brought her down. Not seeing them was.

Let me be clear: Seeing someone’s hidden drivers doesn’t let them off the hook. Laura was responsible for how she treated people, and Elizabeth Holmes was convicted for what she did.

But labels like “bully,” “fraud,” or “villain” close the case. They let us feel safely different from the person we’re judging. Understanding drivers keeps the case open, and that makes change possible. You can’t change what you can’t see.

Seeing your hidden drivers isn’t a label or a verdict. It’s a mirror. And unlike Laura, you don’t need a re-test. You just need the willingness to look.

You Can See Everything promises full access. But none of us can see everything: not in a famous founder, not in the person across the table, and not in ourselves. Not without help and honesty.

All of us have a shadow side. Elizabeth Holmes’s story is an extreme one, but it’s a reminder of how much denial and ego can cost. Whether you’re in over your head at work or hiding the truth from people you care about, you're standing at a choice point. You can dig in deeper, or you can ask for help: from a therapist, a coach, or a trusted friend. Someone who can hold up a mirror and tell you what they see.

You can’t see everything. But you can learn to see yourself.

Bowlby, J. (1980). Attachment and Loss: Vol. 3. Loss: Sadness and Depression. Basic Books.

Edmondson, A. (1999). Psychological safety and learning behavior in work teams. Administrative Science Quarterly, 44(2), 350–383.

Feynman, R. P. (1986). Personal observations on the reliability of the Shuttle. Appendix F, Report of the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident.

Goldsmith, M., & Reiter, M. (2007). What Got You Here Won't Get You There: How Successful People Become Even More Successful. Hyperion.

Kiewitz, C., Restubog, S. L. D., Shoss, M. K., Garcia, P. R. J. M., & Tang, R. L. (2016). Suffering in silence: Investigating the role of fear in the relationship between abusive supervision and defensive silence. Journal of Applied Psychology, 101(5), 731–742.

Mikulincer, M., & Shaver, P. R. (2016). Attachment in Adulthood: Structure, Dynamics, and Change (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

Sutton, R. I. (2010). The Mum Effect and filtering in organizations. Psychology Today.

#4800. Jasion Poki review: The Electric Minibike that packs heavy-duty fun

In our transportation reporting, we rarely come across something as fun as today’s review of the Jasion Poki.

The Poki is a severely overpowered electric minibike that looks like it came from yesteryear. If the power isn’t enough, it also packs some cool tricks, and we’re not (just) talking about wheelies this time.

So taking a look at this bad boy, it just screams fun. It is really low to the ground, has a big, wide seat large enough for 2 people as long as they are under 350lbs total, and has pegs for 2 people and a basket, great for carrying a picnic and an extra helmet.

This thing is built like a tank, and it tips the scales accordingly. Getting this thing in my SUV ruptured a few discs in my back, though its compact nature means it fit quite well. Loosen the handlebars and it is downright compact. But that weight is strangely like 50lbs heavier than I would expect at close to 140lbs.

That also makes the built-in wheelies a little bit more suspect. My son, who is by now becoming an expert at wheelies, found this one to be a bit more difficult than the auto wheelies on bikes like the Anyland or new Yozma IN11.

OK so not only does this little powerhouse get you (and your friend) around town in style and it also makes wheelies a bit easier; but it also has a huge Bluetooth speaker in the back that sounds like a Harley and is all synced up with the actual controller so it sounds real.

Sure, it is a gimmick, but it is a fun one, and it might actually make the low-down bike a little safer since it is going to be out of the sight of most cars.

I love this thing. It is my favorite bike to go to the beach on (and it does well in the sand with those fat tires). But I think there are some big misses here. First of all, it has no business going over 40mph. Not only does it feel scary with those tiny wheels, but speed wobbles puts both the rider a possible second rider at significant risk here. This is a fun bike and it should top out at 20-28mph max. Keep all the torque, just cut out the power at a reasonable top speed.

Also it should weigh a lot less. At 140lbs, it is silly hard to get into the back of a car, which it easily fits in. Making the frame aluminum would go a long way here. Also, if this thing rolled on top of you, it would be a bad day.

Make this thing safer and more portable, and I’d recommend everyone with a beach commute to get one. As it stands, best for responsible adults with strong backs and a Peter Pan complex.

The Poki is currently priced at $1,799, and customers can get 5% off with the code Electrek.

#4799. Gamma-ray burst is one of the brightest in decades

Published Oct 29, 2026 4:15 PM EDT

A gamma-ray burst (GRB) that has confounded astronomers is one of the brightest cosmic light shows in the past 20 years. Although the cosmic explosion first appeared inexplicably weak, researchers now believe it actually shot about one billion years’ worth of solar energy into the cosmos through a beam no thicker than a pencil.

“We see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,” said Roberto Ricci, a radioastronomer at Italy’s National Institute of Astrophysics.

Ricci and his colleague’s findings are detailed in a study recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. On March 10, NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope observed a burst later classified as GRB 260310A. Gamma-ray bursts most frequently occur in the aftermath of a massive star’s collapse. When this happens, powerful jets of matter launch into space close to the speed of light. These jets collide with cosmic gas, which generates afterglows seen across visible light, radio waves, and X-rays.

While GRB 260310A’s flash of light lasted less than one minute, astronomers noted it seemed to produce strangely little energy. This changed within only a few hours, as GRB 260310A’s afterglow brightened so much that it briefly outshone its host galaxy. A few weeks later, the GRB’s X-ray emissions brightened again and then remained observable for months.

“At first, I thought another X-ray source was contaminating our observations. But the brightening really came from the afterglow,” recalled study co-author and astronomer Yu-Han Yang.

Further observations using an international array of observatories and telescopes later confirmed a supernova had indeed prompted a GRB. Early signs indicated that its jet was pointed away from Earth, but while the gamma-ray readings were comparatively basic, both its visible and X-ray measurements ranked among the top one percent in brightness. GRB 260310A also fell within the top five percent for recorded radio brightness. After reviewing the data, astronomers finally realized what was happening.

“We looked at it from a side angle,” explained Yang. “As the jet slowed down, its light became visible over a wider range of angles, allowing us to probe the jet’s shape, from its outer edges toward its inner core.”

Yang compared most GRB observations to looking directly at a flashlight. Although the light is brightest from that perspective, the beam may appear dimmer if it is viewed from further away. Most GRB modeling is calibrated from events detected from a direct vantage point, but GRB 260310A was different.

“This burst gave us a chance to look beyond that glare,” said Yang.

Astronomers theorize that GRB 260310A may have originated from a jet featuring a very narrow, energized core encompassed by wider, slower outflows. If true, the early afterglow hypothetically traces back to the jet’s wings, while the brightening X-ray phase came from the thin core.

Although it took a moment to decipher, GRB 260310A offers a rarely seen window into a gamma-ray burst. Such opportunities are rare, but the team hopes to find more in the near future using even more powerful tools like the recently completed Vera Rubin Observatory.

“We could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder,” added Ricci.

#4798. The Link Between Youth Loneliness and Smartphone Dependency

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

by Dante Lewis-Chan and Robert T. Muller, Ph.D.

According to the 2023 Canadian Health Survey on Children and Youth, the rate of adolescents with poor mental health had more than doubled between 2019 and 2023. The survey assessed mental well-being in 2019, and checked in with those same participants four years later. In the initial survey, about 12 percent of youth aged 12 to 17 had rated their mental health as “fair” or “poor.” This figure rose to 26 percent by 2023.

After the survey’s initial assessment, the COVID-19 pandemic had started. During the pandemic, screen time rose across all age groups. A 2024 study examined this rise and found that students who used social media to cope with the pandemic experienced higher levels of stress, anxiety, and depression. However, this relationship was more pronounced amongst lonelier students.

These findings were echoed in a 2025 study conducted in China. Loneliness, this study found, intensified the relationship between social anxiety and smartphone overdependence in college students. This is further supported by a recent review that suggests a strong association between feelings of isolation and an over-reliance on smartphones.

Jake Ernst, a social worker and psychotherapist in Toronto, explains how chronic loneliness can lead to mental health issues: “For young people, whose brains are still building the scaffolding required for social connection, isolation interrupts the development of essential skills like executive functioning, emotional regulation, and conflict repair."

Ernst also believes that smartphone dependency plays a role in isolation and exacerbates these challenges. He describes it as a paradox: Technology can offer the illusion of connection while actually displacing meaningful, real-world contact. Many young people now spend their time in online spaces, prioritising attention and comparison over genuine connection and weakening their ability to handle real-world social challenges. As they turn more to curated digital interactions instead of practicing real communication, their dependence on these platforms only grows stronger.

Another growing concern in the discussion around youth loneliness is artificial intelligence. There is an emerging phenomenon of people forming emotional and romantic connections with AI. The consequences of such interactions can be alarming, particularly for youth already struggling with their mental health.

A Stanford study conducted in 2025 found that with some commonly used chatbots, like character.ai and Replika, one can elicit inappropriate dialogue concerning topics like self-harm, drug use, and violence. The study notedthat this is especially dangerous for young people, as they are not fully developed and so are more likely to form attachments, even with an AI chatbot.

Chatbots can simulate deep, complex relationships, and while youth recognize that AI isn’t necessarily “alive,” it doesn’t stop them from reciprocating. “AI has mostly intensified smartphone dependency by personalizing it,” Ernst claims. “AI-driven chatbots and companion apps now simulate friendship, intimacy, or care, but without the reciprocity that real relationships require.”

Ernst believes therapeutic interventions can be effective to treat smartphone dependency in youth, as long as “the social health deficit and the digital over-reliance” are addressed. He notes that therapy offers opportunities to develop the ability to co-regulate and process emotions in real-time. It also provides real-world experiences that allow youth to “rediscover the positive aspects of life,” and train the parts of their brains that require those experiences for healthy development.

It can be easy for young people to self-isolate and fall into unhealthy or destructive relationships with technology. But with the right interventions and support from in-person relationships, young people struggling with smartphone dependency can be helped. They can rebuild their sense of connection, regain their social skills, reset their brains, and change their view of the world, both digital and real.

Dante Lewis-Chan is a research student at York University.

Well, it turns out, you might be onto something. Candy companies really do sneakily change their recipes. Our taste buds also change as we get older. So what’s really going on here? Are candy companies changing their recipes or do we just taste things differently now? LB: Okay. Perfect. Let’s, let’s get into it. Are candy companies really messing with our childhood favorites?

SD: They are, 1000 percent. And one of the biggest recent controversies actually involves one of the most iconic Halloween candies, Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups.

SD: I know. Me too. So earlier this year, Brad Reese, the grandson of H.B. Reese, the inventor of Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups, publicly criticized Hershey, the company that makes the candy.

SD: Yeah, it’s kinda wild that there are family candy empires, but, you know, of course there are.

Anyhow, Brad was upset about changes to some of the company’s candy products. Specifically, he pointed to products that use things like compound coatings instead of milk chocolate or peanut butter-style cream instead of actual peanut butter.

LB: So in candy making, what exactly is a compound coating?

SD: It’s a chocolate-like coating that can use vegetable fats in place of some of the cocoa butter you’d find in traditional chocolate, and those substitutions can make a difference in how a candy tastes and feels in your mouth.

LB: The phrase chocolate-like kind of raises a red flag there.

LB: Okay, but here’s the really important question. Did they actually change Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups?

SD: According to Hershey, no. The company says the original Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup recipe hasn’t changed, but it acknowledges that some other Reese’s products, different shapes and sizes and newer varieties, can have different formulations.

LB: Oh, so the classic peanut butter cup shape might be the same, but the other Reese’s candies, like the popular pumpkins or Christmas tree shapes, aren’t necessarily made the same way.

SD: Yes, at least that’s the distinction the company is making. But this isn’t just about Reese’s. Candy companies have been adjusting their recipes for years, and to understand why, Popular Science spoke with Dr. Richard Hartel, a food scientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and he explained that one of the biggest reasons companies change their recipes is pretty straightforward: money.

SD: Yep. Candy manufacturers are a business, and when the price of ingredients goes up, they have a pretty strong incentive to find cheaper alternatives.

But those substitutions aren’t always obvious. Take caramel, for example.

SD: Yes, same. So traditionally, caramel might be made using whole milk and milk fat. But a manufacturer could decide to replace those ingredients with skim milk and a different kind of fat, like vegetable oil or coconut oil.

They might also replace some milk proteins with whey proteins.

SD: Potentially, but it can also change the flavor and texture of the final candy. Because even if two ingredients serve a similar purpose in a recipe, that doesn’t mean they’re gonna taste exactly the same.

LB: Right, and I imagine butter and vegetable oil don’t produce exactly the same caramel just because of chemistry.

You know, it’s like vegan or regular cooking. It’s similar, but different.

SD: Yeah. No, exactly. And the same thing can happen with chocolate. A company might reduce the amount of cocoa in a product while still keeping enough to meet the legal requirement for calling it “chocolate.”

LB: So there are legal requirements for calling it chocolate, kind of like with beer?

SD: There are, yeah. The FDA has what’s called standards of identity for certain foods. Basically, these are rules that determine what ingredients a product needs to contain or how it needs to be made to legally use a particular name. So you can’t necessarily just throw some brown colored sugar and oil together and call it milk chocolate.

LB: So it’s kind of similar to that question of if almond milk can really be called “milk.” Yes. Yeah, I guess it is kind of assuring that there are some sort of standards here.

SD: Oh, yeah. No, those standards still leave manufacturers, though, room to adjust the recipes. And if a company changes its ingredients while staying within those legal requirements, it generally doesn’t have to make some big public announcement or even change their ingredient list.

LB: Right, so there’s not gonna be a big press release saying, “Attention candy lovers, we’ve slightly reduced the cocoa content of your favorite chocolate bar.”

SD: Exactly, and that’s part of what makes this whole thing so sneaky. Because according to Hartel, some of these recipe changes are so subtle that even trained testers might not notice them.

LB: Really? So like even those lucky people whose job it is to literally taste things?

SD: Yep. Imagine you have a candy bar, you know, you’ve eaten your whole life. One year the company makes a tiny adjustment to the recipe. You probably don’t notice. The next year they make another tiny adjustment. Again, you probably don’t notice.

But if you keep doing that over 10 years or 20 years…

LB: Okay, so that explains why a candy bar might taste different now. But here’s what I’m wondering. If people notice these changes and don’t like them, why don’t companies just go back to the original recipes?

SD: Yeah, well that brings us to one of the most famous disasters in the history of food marketing: New Coke.

SD: So back in 1985, Coca-Cola decided to change its signature soda formula, and the company had actually done taste testing beforehand. In blind taste tests, people often preferred sweeter Pepsi over Coke. So Coca-Cola introduced a new sweeter version of its drink.

LB: Which as we now know, people famously hated.

SD: Hated it. And it’s all because of something called the Pepsi paradox. Basically, there’s a difference between tasting a tiny sip of something and actually consuming an entire serving. A sweeter drink might win in a quick sip test, but that doesn’t necessarily mean people want to drink a whole can.

LB: Right. That makes sense. Like if one bite of something is super sweet, it might be delicious—

LB: —but after 10 bites you might be completely over it.

SD: Yeah, and that’s a big challenge for food companies because just because a new recipe performs well in a taste test doesn’t mean consumers will actually prefer it in their everyday lives.

And with New Coke there was another huge factor.

LB: Okay. If it’s not money, I’m gonna guess it’s nostalgia.

SD: Nostalgia. People were attached to the original Coca-Cola. It wasn’t just about how the soda tasted. It was about the memories and feelings associated with it.

LB: All right, and that brings us right back to Halloween candy.

SD: Yeah. When you eat a Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup or a Hershey’s bar, you’re not necessarily just tasting chocolate and sugar and peanut butter.

LB: You might also be remembering the fun of trick-or-treating as a kid, dumping your candy all over the living room floor and trading with your siblings.

SD: Or in my case, hiding an entire year’s supply of candy under my bed.

LB: Hey, I now think it’s very important to have a secret candy bunker.

SD: Look, I concur. And that brings us to another important part of this mystery because even if a candy company hasn’t changed its recipe at all, there’s still something else that could be changing.

SD: Us. Our sense of taste isn’t necessarily the same throughout our lives.

As we get older, our ability to perceive flavors can change, and one reason is that our taste buds don’t regenerate quite as quickly as they used to.

LB: So even if I’m eating a Milky Way, I might experience it differently now.

SD: Right, even if it’s the same exact Milky Way. And it’s not just aging. Our environment and experiences also affect how we perceive taste.

So the way you experience a Milky Way today might be different from the way you experienced it as a kid, even if the recipe is identical.

LB: Okay, so with this mystery, we’ve now got two possible culprits: the candy companies are changing the recipes, and our taste buds are changing too.

SD: And both things can be true at the same time, which makes it difficult to know whether your beloved Milky Way or addictive Nerds actually taste different or whether you just remember it tasting different.

LB: So basically, no matter how much we want to, we’re never getting that exact childhood Halloween candy experience back, no matter how much we try.

SD: I know, but there’s a little good news. Candy companies do sometimes listen when people complain about changes. In fact, Hershey has announced plans to bring back older recipes for some of its products, including certain miniature Easter candies.

LB: Okay, that helps. So there’s some hope.

SD: There is, but Hershey will still experiment with new formulas for other products, so I wouldn’t expect every candy to suddenly taste exactly the way it did in 1998.

SD: But here’s the big takeaway. If you’ve bitten into your favorite childhood candy and thought, “This isn’t as good as it used to be,” you might actually be onto something.

Manufacturers really do change the recipes. Sometimes those changes are tiny, and sometimes they accumulate over decades, but our own taste perception changes too. So the answer to whether candy tastes different now is—

SD: It really is. But before we wrap up this very sweet episode, there’s one thing I want to get to the bottom of because we spent this whole episode talking about how our favorite childhood candies might be changing, but what would someone who tastes food for a living think?

LB: I feel like we need to bring in the expert here.

SD: Me too, and luckily, we got a pretty great one. After the break, we’re gonna be joined by Jack Bishop from America’s Test Kitchen.

LB: Excellent. Love America’s Test Kitchen.

And we’re back with Jack Bishop. Jack is the senior content advisor at America’s Test Kitchen, where he’s been part of the team since the very beginning, starting with the launch of Cook’s Illustrated in 1993. He’s also the tasting lab expert on America’s Test Kitchen and Cook’s Country, which means he’s spent decades putting food to the test.

Jack, thank you so much for joining us on Popular Science’s Ask Us Anything podcast.

Jack Bishop: It’s great to be here, Sarah. Thanks for asking me.

SD: Oh, we’re so excited to have you. So Jack, throughout today’s episode, we’ve been investigating whether our favorite childhood candies really taste different than they used to, and I want to start with a personal question.

Was there a candy you absolutely loved growing up that just doesn’t quite taste as good to you today?

JB: —that’s pretty much true for most candies, especially I was a child of the ’60s and ’70s, and so candies were bigger back then. In my mind, the biggest difference is the caramel isn’t as gooey as it used to be when I was a kid.

JB: When you would bite into a Snickers bar, it was almost like a cheese pull. You know, you’d get this great pull, and I feel like that doesn’t happen anymore.

SD: And given your knowledge of food generally, why do you think Snickers taste different?

JB: You know, it’s hard to say because you do the label reading, and it only gets you so far.

JB: —you know, you can tell by the order of the ingredients. If that changes, that could be a real sign. You know, if something has gone up in the ingredient list, that likely means there’s more of it, because ingredients are listed in the order of sort of weight. You know, they’re just using lower quality ingredients in order to keep costs down.

I mean, that’s the overall trend in what I would call supermarket candy.

JB: Is cost is such a big issue, and so many of the inputs have gotten so expensive. And so, you know, using less of the expensive ingredient, switching out, you know, a moderately priced ingredient for a really cheap ingredient. Those are all strategies that could be used to control cost, but they’re not necessarily gonna make something tastier.

SD: Yeah. Yeah, and if, you know, a listener is listening to this and they feel like one of their favorite candies has changed since they were growing up, what would you suggest? How would they go about testing that?

JB: I should start by saying I think taste memories are powerful but unreliable.

JB: So what I mean by that is I can make a certain recipe, and the house fills with an aroma, like I’m thinking of like my grandmother’s lasagna, and if like my brother or sister walks in, it’s like we’re back in my grandmother’s kitchen, and, you know, I’m eight, and my sister’s seven, and my brother’s five again. The food is really triggering powerful emotions.

JB: But, you know, we misremember stuff, and it’s really hard to remember, well, how sweet was this?

JB: Right? How chocolatey was this? Was this really peanut buttery, or have my tastes just changed? And I know for me, you know, I now like 85 percent cacao chocolate.

Well, I didn’t like that as a kid. And so that will color perceptions of things I did eat when I was a kid, and is it not as good as it used to be, or do I not like that anymore? Unless you can get a time machine and somebody can send you a candy bar from, you know, 1972 or whatever year you’d like to go back to, you’re relying on your memory, and your memory’s a little fickle when it comes to food.

SD: Yeah, and we’ve actually been talking a bit in this episode about Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups because they’ve been at the center of this whole conversation about changing candy recipes, and I know America’s Test Kitchen actually has its own recipe for homemade peanut butter cups. So I’m curious, what makes a really great peanut butter cup? Is there something the homemade version can get right that a store-bought candy might not?

JB: Fewer ingredients and better ingredients. So, you know, if you read the label on a Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup, it’s a pretty long ingredient list. Our homemade version starts with milk chocolate and creamy peanut butter that you enrich with a little bit of butter, a little bit of salt, and a little bit of confectioner sugar ‘cause the confectioner sugar will incorporate into the sugar without giving you any sort of grittiness, and that’s it.

It’s really just creamy peanut butter that’s a little sweeter and a little saltier and a little richer than it is straight out of the jar layered with melted chocolate, and you need, don’t need to anything more than put the chocolate in the microwave, 50 percent power to gently melt it, and then you can actually build them.

The easiest way to do this is in a mini muffin tin.

JB: And you can get little liners, and you sort of pipe a layer of chocolate, pipe a layer of peanut butter, and then finish with a layer of chocolate. So the chocolate’s not completely enrobing the peanut butter, but it’s the neatest, easiest way to do it at home, and it eats like…

Well, I won’t say it eats like a Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup ‘cause it’s so much better.

SD: Well, Jack, thank you so much for joining us. I need to go make peanut butter cups apparently. And Jack, if listeners wanna know more about what you’re up to in America’s Test Kitchen, where should they go?

JB: Sure. We’ve got, you know, tastings of milk chocolate, dark chocolate, white chocolate, and you can find all of those results at americastestkitchen.com.

SD: Great. Thank you so much for making the time, Jack.

LB: Wow, I love him so much. And even though I can’t cook to save my life, I kind of want to try that homemade peanut butter cup recipe.

SD: I know, me too. We’ll link it in the show notes.

And if you like our show, leave us a rating and a review.

SD: What’s your favorite candy? Let us know in the comments. Our producer is Alan Haburchak, and this week’s episode was based on an article written for Popular Science by Andrew Coletti.

LB: Thank you, team, thank you, candy, and thank you everyone for listening.

SD: And one more time, if you want something you’ve always wondered about explained on a future episode, go to popsci.com/ask and click the “Ask Us” link. Until next time, keep the questions coming, and may your candy stay mice-free.

LB: I’m still sad about Baby Sarah’s candy stash.

#4796. How to Support a Child Interested in STEM

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Research study after research study shows the importance of parent and family support for sparking kids’ interests in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) and then helping them stay interested and succeed in STEM as they grow. But how exactly do parents provide helpful support?

A recent study from my team of researchers at Michigan State University (Dorrance Hall et al., 2025) reports on how parents support girls pursuing STEM and women majoring in STEM in college. We interviewed Black, Latina, and white women majoring in STEM across the United States and asked them about the STEM-related support they received while growing up. The findings identify five ways parents can provide much-needed support throughout childhood and adolescence.

Advice, or instrumental support, was the most commonly reported type of support received from parents. Parental advice was useful for navigating important decisions like choosing a major and career path. Parents suggested majors and careers, told girls how to apply for college, provided study tips, and shared job and internship postings. Women appreciated advice that was clear, relevant to their interests, and concrete as opposed to general. They disliked advice that focused on what the parents wanted them to do over their own interests.

Another major way parents can support their children’s interests in STEM is to provide resources such as STEM books and materials, enroll them in after-school activities, and take them to museums. Women reflected on more surprising forms of support that do not cost a lot of money as well—things like cooking meals for them so they could focus on their homework, giving them rides to and from classes, and investing their time to help with challenging assignments.

Parents can provide comfort, empathy, and emotional support as they cope with the challenges of pursuing STEM. Challenges, such as feeling like they don’t belong in their classes or activities and not seeing themselves as scientists in online representations (just to name a few), are amplified for women and people in other underrepresented groups. Children in these groups likely need additional support to succeed in STEM.

Fortunately, there are a lot of ways parents can provide emotional support, starting with comfort and empathy. Emotional support has physiological and emotional health benefits, and parents can provide it even if they have very limited knowledge about STEM. Simply validating that STEM is hard and that the challenges their children are facing are stressful can go a long way. Parents can also help their children gain perspective by reminding them why they are pursuing STEM, that grades only matter so much, and that a semester or school year is temporary. Parents can talk about their children’s skills and their confidence in their kids’ ability to succeed.

Similar to emotional support, parents can encourage and affirm their children’s strengths by providing esteem support. To do this, parents can express pride in their kids’ accomplishments, remind them they are smart, and show them they believe in them to boost their confidence. This type of support can improve self-esteem and well-being and protect against self-doubt.

Parents can also help their children network with others and teach them to ask for help when they need it. Women shared that their parents used their networks to introduce them to new opportunities or help them find the information they needed when the parents did not personally know how to help them. Parents found other adults who had firsthand knowledge about the industry their child was interested in or showed their children how to ask others for help.

Women majoring in STEM described a lot of different things their parents said or did as supportive. This shows that parents have a lot of choice when it comes to how to best support their child. There was not a one-size-fits-all way to be supportive. Instead, parents should stay attuned to what their child needs at their current developmental stage and think about what would be most helpful for the specific challenges they are facing.

Parents can improve their support by making their advice specific and relevant to their child. This could look like saying, “I remember you telling me you were interested in learning about the different types of engineering. Let’s check out these programs that introduce kids to a wide variety of things engineers can do.”

Even if the support a parent gives is not exactly what is needed at the time, women in our study told us that the simple act of receiving support was helpful. Parents showing up, listening, reaching out, and making an effort go a long way in helping women succeed in STEM.

Dorrance Hall, E., Watson, O., Zhang, Y., Wolfe, B.H., Cui, X., Edwards, A.L., Liu, R., & Lawlor, D. (2025). Parental support content and quality: Supporting girls’ and women’s interest and persistence in STEM. International Journal of Gender, Science and Technology, 17(1), 17-43. https://genderandset.open.ac.uk/index.php/genderandset/article/view/1570/1344

Dorrance-Hall, E., Zhang, Y., Edwards, A. L., Wolfe, B. H., Watson, O., Morales, N., & Valdes, P. (2025). STEM career interest development and persistence: what parents do, say, and should say. Annals of the International Communication Association. https://doi.org/10.1093/anncom/wlaf018

Starr, C. R., Tulagan, N., & Simpkins, S. D. (2022). Black and Latinx adolescents’ STEM motivational beliefs: A systematic review of the literature on parent STEM support. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 1877–1917. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09700-6

Holmstrom, A. J. (2012). What helps–and what doesn’t–when self-esteem is threatened?: Retrospective reports of esteem support. Communication Studies, 63(1), 77–98. https://doi.org/10.1080/10510974.2011.586399

#4795. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

#4794. World War II’s baby gas masks are as unnerving as you’d imagine

Published Oct 30, 2026 9:54 AM EDT

Time forgets the vast majority of inventions—usually for good reason. As parents and children everywhere get ready for trick-or-treating, we’d like to turn your attention to one such invention: the baby gas mask.

In the November 1938 issue of Popular Science, “a doll demonstrates the use of the baby gas mask” in an undeniably creepy image. The word mask is perhaps a misnomer here, because this contraption actually completely engulfs the baby as “filtered air is pumped in with an artificial lung.”

These baby gas masks were developed at a time when around the world people feared another world war would—and eventually did—ignite. The brief story on the contraption reads, “Babies are protected from poison gas in case of a wartime attack” by these novel masks.

But it’s still hard to imagine any baby well-behaved enough to sit inside such a creepy invention. Nonetheless, the French inventors behind the technology thought this would be a good idea—even a profitable one. And in the lead up to World War II, the baby gas mask briefly caught on, with several vintage photographs showing off different iterations of the device.

In one 1937 image (featured above), a woman and young toddler both sport gas masks in Germany.

There’s also a whole slew of children and babies wearing gas masks in vintage photographs from England. One photograph (below) shows how a baby gas mask, also known as a hood, worked as a woman demonstrates using the contraption at the historic Holborn Town Hall in London, England.

This particular design took three years to develop. An infant is placed inside a fabric hood featuring a large cellulose acetate window. A drawstring cinches the hood at the infant’s waist, so that the arms, shoulders, and head are completely contained. An adult then operates a rubber bellows to filter air into the hood.

There was apparently no time limit for how long a child could be kept inside the airtight mask—as long as air was steadily pumped in, of course. As to whether the infant enjoyed the contraption, no one could ask.

Another photograph taken (fittingly) during Halloween season, on October 20, 1937, at Dr. Barnardo’s nursery home in Hawkhurst, Kent, England, shows several toddlers in a more traditional face gas mask. The home was actually nicknamed the Babies’ Castle. It originally opened in 1883, after a Mr. Theodore Moillet donated two adjacent mansions and an acre of meadowland for the nursery.

Yet another photograph from England shows several mothers holding babies fitted with the hood-style gas mask designed by the Royal Air Force.

Hospitals in England were also fitted with baby gas masks, and one 1940 photograph shows several nurses testing out the new technology.

One little girl named Jean Panter even convinced her father to make her doll a gas mask. This photograph of little Jean with her doll was taken in England on February 11, 1938, shortly before World War II began. The fact that even a young girl wanted a gas mask for her beloved toy certainly speaks to how much fears of poison gas permeated society before and during World War II.

In 1938, Dr. Jacques Marie Le Mée (sometimes spelled La Mee or Le-Mee), the head physician at the Hôpital Necker-Enfants-Malades in Paris, developed another type of baby gas mask. In fact, the hospital Le Mée worked at is the oldest children’s hospital in the Western world, initially founded in 1801 as Hôpital des Enfants Malades.

In one 1939 photograph, several women and their babies don Le Mée’s baby gas mask in a Parisian square. As opposed to the baby gas hoods on display in vintage English photographs, Le Mée’s invention envelopes the entire baby’s body. Even the baby’s legs will get clean air.

Even though the November 1938 issue of Popular Science says the baby gas mask gracing its pages was developed in France, it’s markedly different to the above photograph of Le Mée’s baby gas mask.

In this design, the window is larger and it’s also unclear how the baby gas mask cinches or becomes airtight around the infant.

Someone holding the child pumps fresh air into the hood-style gas mask. “The person holding the infant controls the amount of fresh air entering the [baby] shelter by pressing on the rubber-lung unit,” the short story in the magazine reads.

But even in dark times, children always find a way to have fun. In one delightful comment on a BBC story about baby gas masks, one reader, William Irwin, remembers having “endless fun playing ‘divers’ with one” baby gas mask.

“We were so far removed from bombing risk areas so I do not believe I was ever put into it as a war-baby. It gave me the interest to eventually become a scuba sports diver.”

Even though this technology thankfully fell by the wayside and seems very strange to modern eyes, it still offers us a lot to think about. The inventions that come out of hard times can even inspire—at least if you’re William Irwin.

In That Time When, Popular Science tells the weirdest, most surprising, and little-known stories that shaped science, engineering, and innovation.

#4792. Build a Career Around Being Yourself

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

We are living through an era of doubts about what constitutes reality, and trepidation about the effects AI will have on jobs and livelihoods. That leads to an important question: how can you build a career around being yourself?

Peter Drucker, the father of modern management (1909-2005), was a master at tapping into his own uniqueness while encouraging people to examine what made them unique and valuable to others. Nearly sixty years ago, in his classic book The Effective Executive, he wrote that “the effective executive tries to be himself; he does not pretend to be someone else. He looks at his own performance and at his own results and tries to discern a pattern.”

Consider what made Drucker unique. Many people, then and now, engaged in the same activities as his: writing, teaching, and consulting. But nobody did it quite like him, and it is why people worldwide continue to pay attention to what he wrote, taught, and advised.

Over a period of many years, people wanted to be in Drucker’s presence, either when he gave presentations and keynotes, lectures in classes and at conferences, or in one-on-one meetings, especially for his consulting clients. They wanted access to his mind, not only for in-person activities, but in the numerous books and articles he wrote in a career spanning more than 70 years.

We can strive for similar attention and effects, even though we are unlikely to have the same magnitude, as we express our individuality in daily activities and planning for the future. Making the most of being yourself is a deceptively simple concept, yet is not necessarily easy to carry out.

We can work on how we express what makes us unique and valuable in our own lives and work, and how we interact with other people. It means being genuine, sincere, and authentic, with a positive and resourceful attitude.

Being the most complete expression of yourself helps you to avoid the trap of comparing yourself to others, or engaging in unhelpful thoughts like impostor syndrome, with the nagging feeling that you don’t deserve or belong in your role. Taking advantage of, and looking for the fullest expression of our individuality and its potential requires self-awareness, confidence, high quality, and self-efficacy.

If you want to build a career revolving around being yourself, make and review lists of areas of strength that can transcend disciplines and be applied to a variety of roles, and not just one particular job.

For example, here are ten examples of personal/professional excellence qualities:

Everyone will have their own unique list, based on personal interests and experience; and talents they were born with, or developed early or later in life.

These areas of excellence can still be strengthened in the future. Being yourself does not mean remaining static; like Drucker, you should be open to change and to engage in self-development as you move into an uncertain future. One reason he remained at the top of his various professions for so many years is that he engaged in regular and fairly rigorous self-study projects (from world history to the works of Shakespeare). Everyone is a work in progress.

Being aware of our human strengths can also help other people to take advantage of being themselves. For instance, many of the examples of personal excellence listed above (e.g. listening, empathy and compassion, teaching, and leadership) lend themselves to collaborating with others to aid in their own self-discovery process.

“To be a leader today,” the leadership coach and author Hortense le Gentil recently wrote, “is not to compete with the machine. It is to become more human. To do the things that cannot be coded or digitized. Sure, we can tell AI to write with more empathy and compassion. But the output remains a simulation of human emotion.”

Generative AI is awe-inspiring. In the past four years, we’ve witnessed astonishing achievements. Yet AI can’t copy exactly what we do, who we are, or what makes us unique. How can we maintain and continue to develop that advantage, with AI’s inevitable improvements in the future?

Peter F. Drucker: The Effective Executive: The Definitive Guide to Getting the Right Things Done, 50th anniversary edition (Harper Business, 2017)

Hortense le Gentil: “On Being More Human in the Age of the Machine,” Leader to Leader, Issue 122, Fall 2026

#4791. Waymo picks Toyota bZ4X as its next robotaxi, starting in Japan in 2027

Waymo is adding the Toyota bZ4X to its robotaxi lineup. Toyota will build a custom version of the electric SUV with the Waymo Driver integrated right on the line in Japan, and a test fleet will start operating there in 2027.

It’s the first actual vehicle to come out of the partnership the two companies signed last year. And it gives Waymo a Japanese-built car for its Tokyo launch, with the UK and other markets to follow.

When Waymo and Toyota first announced their deal in April 2025, it was a preliminary agreement to “explore” working together on autonomous driving, including in personally owned vehicles. Lots of intent, no product.

Now there’s a product. According to Waymo’s announcement, Toyota will produce the vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, and Waymo’s self-driving hardware will be installed and integrated at that same site instead of being retrofitted somewhere else.

The robotaxi bZ4X gets a few rider-focused changes: extra rear legroom, automatic doors, a power liftgate, and ambient lighting. Waymo didn’t share sensor specs, unit volumes, or what each vehicle costs.

Operations in 2027 are about testing and validating the autonomous bZ4X fleet in Japan. The UK and “other Waymo markets” come in later years, with no dates attached.

The two companies also say they’ll keep working on autonomous tech for Toyota’s personal vehicles, plus safety projects with Woven by Toyota, the automaker’s software arm.

Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov said that “Toyota’s commitment to zero traffic accidents resonates deeply with us at Waymo.”

The timing lines up with Waymo’s Japan plans. In September, Waymo said it’s targeting fully driverless commercial rides in Tokyo in 2027 with taxi operator Nihon Kotsu and ride-hailing app GO, scaling to about 100 vehicles, pending regulatory approval.

In the US, Waymo’s fleet is still mostly made up of Jaguar I-Pace SUVs, a model Jaguar no longer produces. It’s been adding the Zeekr-built Ojai van and the Hyundai Ioniq 5, and Hyundai is reportedly in talks to supply up to 50,000 Ioniq 5 robotaxis by 2028.

The bZ4X makes four. It isn’t Toyota’s first robotaxi bZ4X either: Toyota and Pony.ai started mass-producing bZ4X-based robotaxis in China earlier this year.

For US readers, the refreshed model is sold here simply as the Toyota bZ, starting at $34,900. A cheap, high-volume base vehicle matters a lot when you’re trying to scale a fleet.

And Waymo is scaling. It now does over 500,000 paid rides a week across 15 US metros, and it picked Toronto as its first Canadian city earlier this month, with riders targeted for 2028.

This is a big one, even if the bZ4X is about as exciting as a toaster.

Waymo’s biggest constraint right now is cars. It has been running a fleet built on a discontinued Jaguar, and every new automaker it signs adds manufacturing capacity it doesn’t have to build itself. Toyota is the world’s best-selling automaker. Having it build Waymo-ready vehicles on its own assembly line is exactly the kind of industrial partner Waymo needed.

If Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning a personal vehicle, they are likely working on it. It doesn’t mean that it is going to happen but it’s obviously an avenue that they are both willing to explore. If things work out and they are actually able to bring a fully autonomous vehicle to market, that’s an extremely significant advantage from a top legacy car manufacturer that ultimately changes the game for Toyota and could potentially put them in the middle of the competition with other EV manufacturers.

Yes, the bZ4X had a rough start (Toyota recalled the first batch in 2022 because the wheels could come off). But it has come a long way now – becoming boring and reliable. And for a robotaxi, boring and reliable is the whole point.

Compare that with Tesla’s approach: a two-seat Cybercab with no steering wheel, built in-house, with a self-certified autonomy stack that still isn’t operating at anything close to Waymo’s scale. Waymo keeps plugging its driver into existing EVs from established automakers and expanding city by city. So far, that’s working.

The way it is looking now. It sounds like Toyota will take over manufacturing Waymo driver cars for right-hand-drive markets. But what interests me most is the personal-vehicle angle. Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning it, but there’s still nothing concrete. If Toyota actually puts the Waymo Driver in a car you can buy, Tesla’s FSD Supervised pitch gets a lot harder to sell. Will that happen before the end of the decade? Who knows.

#4790. Seven young condors released in northern California

Published Oct 30, 2026 11:12 AM EDT

In 1986, there wasn’t a single California condor (Gymnogyps californianus) left in the wild. Thankfully, it wasn’t because the birds of prey had gone extinct, but they were getting close. In the 1980s, there were fewer than two dozen condors remaining in the wild. That’s why the United States Fish and Wildlife Service moved them into a captive breeding and release program.

Now, the Northern California Condor Restoration Program has released seven young condors into the wild in Yurok Country, close to the Oregon border, according to a statement emailed to Popular Science. One of the birds is particularly special—the condor represents the 200th California condor hatched at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park to be released into the wild. In total, the safari park has hatched 291 condors since 1982.

The seven recently released condors will join 26 other condors already enjoying the Yurok Country site. It’s the most recently established California condor release site, and received its first released condors in 2022. The NCCRP is a collaboration between the Yurok Tribe and the Redwood National and State Parks.

“Condor releases are critical to achieving our ultimate goal- to reestablish a self-sustaining condor population in the wild,” Joe Burnett, California Condor Recovery Program Manager at the Ventana Wildlife Society in California, previously told Popular Science.

It was Burnett that taught us about an unexpected behavior in young condors: the “zoomies” we more frequently associate with dogs.

“We observe the zoomies in both captive and wild condors. It’s just a sudden expression of pure excitement for young condors and very fun to watch,” Burnett explained at the time. “They just can’t contain themselves and totally let loose. They hop, run in circles, or flap around, or all the above! It’s just pure fun!”

It’s unclear whether the special “200th” bird experienced such a display. Either way, the release is happy news. There are now seven more condors in the wild, when only a few years ago there were none.

#4789. Healthgrades Announces Top Hospitals for Specialty Care, Outpatient Procedures

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Hospital ratings have become an important resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades announced the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

New research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

Around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” said Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Navigating the complex healthcare system can feel daunting, but taking a proactive stance to understand where to access superior care can enhance your healthcare journey and overall experience. The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”

Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.

Finding high quality care is important, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.

According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:

“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers said.

“Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.

“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”

Biggers said that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:

Hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.

“Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers said.

“Equally important, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”

Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:

Biggers said that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.

“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she said.

Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.

The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.

Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.

Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.

“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.

“While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.

Healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.

Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

From 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers said.

“Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she said.

Ratings can help patients ask better questions and compare options, but they should complement — not replace — clinical guidance and informed decision making.

#4788. Volkswagen hits pause on the Golf EV as it faces an ‘urgent need for action’

Volkswagen has put the electric Golf on hold for now as it faces growing pressure to cut costs.

“We cannot afford to lose any time and must act quickly and decisively,” Volkswagen Group CFO and COO Arno Antlitz warned after the company reported its largest quarterly loss since the “Dieselgate” scandal in 2015 on Thursday.

VW Group’s operating loss swelled to €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter because of a write-down of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and lower profit margins on electric vehicles.

As part of its latest cost-control efforts, Volkswagen is pausing development of the all-electric Golf at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said in an internal memo Reuters reviewed on Friday. The Wolfsburg plant, or the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Schäfer said the “decision was really not an easy one for us,” knowing what the Golf means to Wolfsburg.

The decision comes after Volkswagen’s Supervisory Board approved its restructuring strategy, “Future Plan 2030,” last month, which includes reducing its global workforce by 100,000, trimming its lineup, and closing several plants in Germany.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer confirmed earlier this year that the electric hatch will be delayed until closer to 2030.

It should be noted that they paid out dividends of 2.6 billion in August. Most of it went to 3 majority shareholders. But they used a clever accounting trick to delay the losses till now, just before talks with unions about pay.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected.

The electric Golf, which is expected to arrive as the ID. Golf, will be one of the first vehicles based on the new platform.

While development is on hold, VW’s works council said the pause will not delay the Golf EV’s launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030.

Volkswagen will begin building the electric Golf in Wolfsburg closer to the end of the decade, while production of the gas-powered model will move to Mexico in 2027.
