#4787. How the 4 Cs Destroy Intimacy and How You Can Repair It

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Many couples come into my office believing that their conflicts are about mundane things, such as who should load the dishwasher or how to reduce their credit card bills, and many of them learn that the real underlying problems are trust, safety, and security. Intimacy is a fragile agreement that is renewed daily, and the signifiers that are read subconsciously by both partners can cause them to feel disrespected and unsupported, which destroys the desire to be intimate.

In his book Role Mate to Soul Mate, relationship expert Dr. Warren Farrell argues that four relatively normal yet bad habits — criticism, complaining, controlling, and complacency — are detrimental to intimacy long before either partner notices that the relationship has grown stale. I love how Dr. Farrell provides a practical map of exactly where the erosion begins (earlier than you think) for couples as well as the clinicians who work with them.

Each of what Dr. Farrell calls “the Four Cs” operates through a distinct psychological mechanism that subtly provides the recipient with a subconscious reason to pull back:

I worked with a couple in which the husband was very adept at complimenting his wife on her domestic competence while saying very little about the marriage itself — she would say that he was polite but that he had low EQ. By the time they came to me, she described feeling more like a competent maid (or his mother) than a partner. Her subconscious response was to lose interest in being intimate because of this dynamic that he unwittingly established: not appreciating her as a person, but just for the tasks she performed. She wanted to be appreciated for her beauty, intellect, being fun, and being a good mother, and not just for maintaining a clean house. Actually, with the best intentions, the husband’s positive reinforcement for cleaning landed with the wife as “controlling.” It appeared that the husband had a subconscious imprint of gender roles in his head, and his expectations only rewarded his wife when she behaved accordingly. Dr. Farrell believes that damage can accumulate even when nothing overtly dramatic appears to be happening, and this is what I have witnessed in sessions with couples.

Over the past eighteen years as a clinician, I have seen over and over how criticism, complaining, controlling, and complacency can destroy intimacy. Couples usually need guidance on how to communicate authentically and compassionately with each other, and this usually requires blocking out time and framing weekly “Caring and Sharing” sessions outside of therapy, as Dr. Farrell suggests. Once each partner knows there is time set aside each week to make each of them feel fully heard — even if they disagree with each other — the “walking on eggshells” and emotional distance are replaced by feeling more emotionally safe, secure, connected, deeply in love, free to be vulnerable, and thus more intimate. Books such as Role Mate to Soul Mate provide tools to help couples identify their criticism, complaining, controlling, and complacency and make changes to rebuild love and intimacy.

Farrell, W. (2024). Role mate to soul mate: The seven secrets to lifelong love. BenBella Books.

#4786. Male black bear ‘Nugget’ wins Introvert Award for his adorable hiding technique

Published Oct 30, 2026 11:48 AM EDT

Like the patient Paul, a male black bear (Ursus americanus) named Nugget would rather hang back alone than jump right into the salmon fest. For his solo tendencies, the team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded Nugget the 2026 Introvert Award.

“For much of the season, Nugget could be seen wedged between rocks by lower falls,” the U.S. Forest Service team writes. “If you saw a furry, black head with glassy eyes poking out of a crack—that’s Nugget! You could also find him perched on a rock waiting for his turn to fish in the lower falls hierarchy; afraid to assert his dominance in the crowd.”

Nugget was first spotted in the area only two years ago, and is beloved for his small size. He has a reddish coat that shifts to black later in the season. Nugget is often described as “scrappy.” He mostly scavenged during his first season at the creek, but slowly learned to catch salmon.

“The pristine ecosystem around Anan Creek allows even small, scrappy bears like Nugget to thrive,” the Rangers write.

The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest are currently doling out the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

The nation’s largest national forest, Tongass covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 known bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their chunky counterparts further north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear and explore.org’s cameras also broadcast live streams of their antics.

#4784. 6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study shows an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

The researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is important to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she said.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” said Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

The researchers found that black tea showed a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” said Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

#4783. World’s tallest Day of the Dead sculpture erected in Mexico City

Published Oct 30, 2026 12:30 PM EDT

Mexico City has broken a Guinness World Record during its preparations for this year’s Day of the Dead (Día de los Muertos) celebrations. At nearly 110 feet tall, the colorful sculpture of a female skeleton currently standing in the capital city’s town square (the Zócalo) is officially the world’s tallest La Catrina monument. The roughly 11-story project made from steel and fiberglass required about 140 people to assemble, and overshadows the town of Puerto Vallarta’s 92.3-foot Catrina built back in 2023. The height isn’t the only impressive aspect, either. Her purple dress measures over 88 feet long, while the memorial altar (called an ofrenda) is surrounded by an estimated 70,00 marigold plants grown in the nearby Xochimilco borough.

Observed each year on November 1 and 2, Mexico’s Day of the Dead is famously dedicated to celebrating and honoring deceased family members and loved ones. Historians are divided on its exact origins—while some researchers contend it possesses genuine Indigenous pre-Hispanic roots, others argue the holiday is a more recent rebrand of Spanish traditions intended to promote cultural pride. Regardless of the answer, Day of the Dead has evolved into one of the country’s most popular and iconic observances. Every year, celebrants often wear skeleton-themed costumes and construct ofrendas, while families and friends gather to fondly recall the departed.

Apart from its size, Mexico City’s record-breaking sculpture is a relatively traditional example of La Catrina, one of Day of the Dead’s most recognizable figures. It’s also much easier to trace La Catrina’s history compared to the holiday’s origins. The figure is based on early 20th century Mexican illustrator José Guadalupe Posada’s most famous work, “La Calavera Catrina” ( or “The Elegant Skull”). Posada’s illustration was released posthumously, and depicts a woman’s skeleton dressed in stylish clothing. Art historians widely view “La Calavera Catrina” as a critique of upper-class Mexican women who attempted to mirror European fashions of the era. Posada’s piece was later expanded upon by the muralist Diego Rivera in 1946-1947.

Similarly inspired iconography has since become a mainstay of Day of the Dead celebrations. La Catrina sculptures like the new record breaker in Mexico City are frequently surrounded by marigolds. Also known as cempasúchil, the flowers are traditionally believed to help guide spirits home with their scent and colorful petals.

Like life itself, Mexico City’s building-sized La Catrina is only temporary. Admirers will be able to visit the installation and its altar only until November 2.

#4781. When Elephants Grieve, What Are They Thinking and Feeling?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

There's little doubt that elephants and many other animals experience grief. Elephants often are the "poster animals" for their profound response to the death of other elephants, something I observed after the death of an elephant matriarch in the Samburu National Reserve along with elephant expert Dr. Iain Douglas-Hamilton. I could literally feel their grief and the depth of their loss. Psychologists Drs. Dustin Kieschnick and Katie Lawlor's research on this important topic speaks to many current questions of interest about this important and hot topic.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you decide to study grief in elephants?

Dustin Kieschnick and Katie Lawlor: Our interest in elephant grief grew from our work as psychologists and our longstanding curiosity about the emotional lives of animals. Much of our professional work has centered on grief, attachment, and the ways people navigate loss, including the loss of beloved companion animals. Through this work, we've come to appreciate that grief is, in many ways, a reflection of love and attachment. It speaks to the significance of relationships.

That led us to ask: If grief emerges from attachment, memory, and the disruption of social bonds, why assume it is exclusively human?

Elephants are especially compelling because of their complex, multigenerational societies, enduring relationships, and remarkable communication. Our interest deepened through our connection with Dr. Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell and a visit to Mushara, a research waterhole in Namibia's Etosha National Park. Witnessing elephants interact in their natural environment was profoundly moving.

Our work draws on decades of field research to explore what elephant responses to death might reveal about attachment, memory, and loss. That said, scientific humility is essential: each species must be understood within its own biological, social, and ecological context.

MB: Who do you hope to reach with your research?

DK/KL: People who have never considered that wildlife might respond to loss in ways resembling grief. Many of us readily recognize the attachments of dogs and cats, yet don't always extend that understanding to wild animals.

We also hope to reach psychologists, educators, conservationists, and policymakers. For conservation, protecting elephants means more than maintaining population numbers. It also means considering family structures, relationships, and knowledge passed between generations.

Most importantly, we hope readers will see animals through a more compassionate and thoughtful lens. The more we understand their social lives, the harder it becomes to regard them solely as populations to manage. Greater understanding can inspire not only empathy, but also a deeper sense of responsibility for how we coexist with other species.

MB: What are some of your major findings and major messages?

DK/KL: One striking finding is elephants' sustained interest in the dead. Researchers have observed them touching bodies with their trunks, investigating bones, remaining near remains, and sometimes revisiting death sites. These behaviors suggest that death has social and behavioral significance beyond the immediate moment.

Equally important is the complexity of elephant relationships. Families depend on communication, memory, and intergenerational learning. The death of a matriarch can mean not only the loss of an individual, but also the loss of ecological knowledge that helps others survive.

Elephant brain structures associated with memory and social-emotional processing offer relevant biological context, although anatomy alone cannot establish what an elephant feels. And elephants are not alone: researchers have observed potentially grief-related responses to death in chimpanzees, orcas, and other species. Such observations are studied within comparative thanatology, the interdisciplinary study of how animals respond to death.

Our central message is that an elephant's death can affect an entire social world: relationships may be disrupted, knowledge lost, and surviving animals profoundly affected.

MB: How does your work differ from others concerned with these topics?

DK/KL: We see our contribution as complementary to the work of field biologists, ethologists, and neuroscientists. Their observations provide the essential evidence. We bring those findings into conversation with psychology, grief research, and animal ethics.

In particular, we ask what our understanding of attachment and bereavement might help us recognize in other species, while remaining cautious about direct comparisons. We also ask what ethical responsibilities follow when research shows that animals maintain lasting relationships and experience social disruption following death.

What should that mean for conservation decisions, human-wildlife conflict, and the care of elephants in captivity? We hope to honor the contributions of field researchers by making these questions accessible and relevant to how we understand and treat other animals.

MB: Are you hopeful that, as people learn about grief in elephants and other animals, they will use this information on behalf of the animals?

DK/KL: Absolutely. How we understand animals influences how we treat them.

Conservation has rightly emphasized habitat protection and population survival. But with highly social species, numbers tell only part of the story. An elephant killed by poachers may also be a mother, a companion, or a matriarch carrying decades of ecological knowledge. Her death may have consequences throughout the group. Likewise, caring for elephants in captivity requires attention not only to physical health, but also to social relationships and opportunities for natural behavior.

We hope this research encourages greater humility, curiosity, and compassion. Rather than judging animals by how closely they resemble humans, we can ask how they experience their own worlds.

Recognizing the possibility of grief in elephants does not require us to say their experience is identical to ours. It asks us to take their relationships seriously. If our work helps even a few people see an elephant as an individual with relationships, memories, and a life that matters, then it has accomplished something meaningful. Ultimately, we hope understanding animals' emotional lives will inspire us to treat them with the dignity and respect they deserve.

In conversation with psychologists Drs. Dustin Kieschnick and Katie Lawlor, Fellows of the Oxford Centre for Animal Ethics.

#4780. In 1841, flesh and blood rained down in Tennessee

Published Oct 30, 2026 1:53 PM EDT

One August day in 1841, near Lebanon, Tennessee, two enslaved people heard the sound of rain pattering on the tobacco leaves around them. But this was no ordinary rain: It was a deep red color. The sky, it seemed, was raining blood. Even more alarming, small pieces of flesh and fat seemed to be raining down, too. The two witnesses took the leaves inside to show their enslaver, Mr. E.M. Chandler, who quickly reported the event to his neighbors.

In an attempt to clear things up, pieces of fallen material were sent to Dr. Gerard Troost, a renowned scientist and collector of natural history specimens. Upon opening the package, Troost noted that it “had the offensive smell of putrid animal matter.” After a thorough analysis, Dr. Troost’s assessment was clear: “There is no doubt but that this substance is animal matter and belongs to our globe.”

The flesh and blood fall near Lebanon in 1841 was far from the only time blood rain or flesh has fallen from the sky, nor was it the last. Both experts and lay people have put forward various explanations for blood rains and flesh falls, including animals being torn up by storms, hoaxes, carcasses dropped by vultures, meteor dust, algal spores, or even red discharge from butterflies.

The 1841 blood rain incident in Lebanon has to be contextualized within the buildup to the Civil War, and a massacre that happened almost exactly 10 years earlier. In 1831, an enslaved carpenter and preacher named Nat Turner in Southampton, Virginia began having visions of “lights in the sky to which the children of darkness gave other names than what they really were—for they were the lights of the Saviour’s hands,” followed by sightings of “drops of blood on the corn, as though it were dew from heaven.”

When Turner later found hieroglyphic marks written in blood on leaves in the woods, he took it as an omen: Shortly afterwards, he led one of the deadliest uprisings of enslaved people in U.S. history. From August 21 to August 23, 1831, Nat Turner and his followers killed 55 white people. In response, local militias and roving mobs killed an unknown number of both enslaved and free Black people. Nat Turner and some of his followers were sentenced to death and executed.

When enslaved people discovered blood on the tobacco leaves in Lebanon in 1841, the fuss was enormous, and echoed Nat Turner’s accounts of bloody rain. Locals in Lebanon wrote about their local blood rain incident in letters to relatives, newspapers from near and far reported on it, and the farm became somewhat of a circus.

A visitor from another town, William F. Cooper, wrote in his journal that “the smell of this fallen matter was very offensive, polluting the whole air.” Cooper also described the extent of the fall as “from 40 to 60 yards in width, and six or eight hundred yards in length,” equivalent to around six to eight football fields.

After Dr. Troost later analyzed the material and determined it was, in fact, animal matter, the flesh fall was reported in the American Journal of Science. Troost’s primary theory was that a strong wind “might have taken up part of an animal which was in a state of decomposition, and have brought it in contact with an electric cloud, in which it was kept in a state of partial fluidity or viscosity.”

After the Lebanon flesh and blood fall, stories of Nat Turner and the slave rebellion were revived in full force. Many white Southerners feared another uprising. On the other hand, Northerners saw the blood rain as a heavenly critique on the practice of slavery.

On September 10, 1841, The Wisconsin Enquirer reported that residents in Northern states had likened the Lebanon event to the blood fall in Virginia that occurred before Nat Turner’s uprising, and “construed the mysterious shower [in Lebanon] into a judgment from heaven, designed to warn the slave-holding states of the iniquity of their traffic in flesh and blood.”

The mystery of the flesh and blood fall in Lebanon was never totally resolved, and was eventually dismissed as a hoax perpetrated by the two enslaved people who witnessed it first. This was later rebutted in The Western Journal of Medicine and Surgery in December 1841.

“People have a need for an explanation, just any explanation, regardless of whether or not it is the explanation,” says Tom Maxwell, writer, blood rain researcher, and host of The Night Parade podcast. “In this case, I think culturally a lot of people needed it to be a hoax.”

Blood rains and flesh falls stretch far back into history. They are mentioned in both The Iliad and the Bible. Philosophers, scientists, and storytellers have described numerous incidents throughout the centuries, including in ancient Rome, medieval Ireland, the 19th century United States, and around the world today.

Nineteenth-century scientists even attempted to find a scientific reason for these falls with microscopes. These scientists could determine “it was always blood. It was always animal material,” says Maxwell. “The question was how did it get where it got, not what it was.” Contemporary scientists have narrowed in on these two separate questions: First, what is falling from the sky, and second, how did it get in the sky?

While blood rains and flesh falls are often discussed together, there are likely different mechanisms behind them. One common explanation for flesh falls lines up with what Troost proposed in 1841: a strong storm, or even vultures, can sweep flesh up into the sky and drop it down later. Strange weather events like this are not unheard of, and fish falls, insect tornadoes, or even frogs falling from the sky have all been documented before.

Blood rain, on the other hand, has a completely different explanation. In these cases, the rain is red because it likely contains dust or microorganisms rather than animal matter. This was hard to detect in the past.

“They didn’t have the science,” says Dr. Patrick McCafferty, a researcher at Chemnitz University of Technology who has studied how myths and literature often record real-world comets, meteor strikes, or other catastrophes. “So [from their perspective] this seems to be something sent by God to punish them.”

The reality is that since Christians were largely familiar with the concept of an impending doomsday and blood rain in the Bible, “They would interpret these things as blood,” says McCafferty. “They’re also primed to look out for these signs of the end of the world.”

Bloody rains studied in the past few decades have given clues as to what the substance may be, at least in some cases. One key example of this is the blood rain that fell in Kerala, India, in 2001.

Researchers collected samples of the red rain, and found it contained algal or seaweed spores, which caused the red coloration. Another research group argued the Kerala blood rain was the result of dust blown over from desert areas in West Asia.

Yet another group asserted that the Kerala blood rain was red because it was full of “bacteria-like material that had been swept to Earth from a passing comet.” They argued that if a comet had broken apart in the Earth’s atmosphere, extraterrestrial particles could have made it into the clouds, raining down as blood-red droplets.

Despite the frequent co-occurrence of meteors or comets and blood rain (a route of investigation also pursued by McCafferty) the explanation has not been widely adopted.

With so many eyewitness accounts of blood rains and flesh falls across the centuries, it’s hard to dismiss the phenomenon. “Chances are, it was real. Chances are, it was caused by something,” says McCafferty. “I’m conscious that things happen that do not have a good explanation.”

When it comes to meat, fat, or red rain falling from the sky, we shouldn’t be too quick to dismiss what it really looks like: flesh and blood. “The classic example is the [French Academy of Sciences] completely dismissing accounts that stones fell from the sky,” says McCafferty.

“So when anybody would come to them with a meteorite, they would say ‘This was hit by thunder or this was hit by lightning. This is a thunderstone. It was hit by lightning. It did not fall from space. It’s stupid to believe stones fall from space.’ And then it turns out that, oh, actually they do.”

Many questions about blood rain and flesh falls remain unanswered. In Maxwell’s opinion, that’s okay: “In the face of the inexplicable,” he says, “I think the most appropriate epistemological response is ‘I don’t know.’”

#4779. Drug-Resistant ‘Superbugs’ Linked to More Than 50,000 Deaths a Year, CDC Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

The updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

The new report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

These findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC said that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), said in a statement.

The CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that currently includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”

“An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he said.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”

“The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” said Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

Cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

Candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

These bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

While those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” said Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” said Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is currently under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing new antibiotics is important.

“You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, said in a statement.

#4777. What Your Team Stops Telling You When Founders Fight

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Nobody said a word about last week's fight with your cofounder. They don't need to. In Monday's all-hands meeting, your team watched you interrupt him. They watched him shut down, and they saw the look on his face. And now they're censoring what they will tell you directly and what they will say behind your back.

One pair of founders I worked with agreed with each other in private. In team meetings, one of them kept undercutting the other in front of the people they'd hired. When the first founder corrected someone's technical work, his cofounder called it micromanagement. Neither of them described what that word meant to them.

The team heard it as permission to ignore the feedback. The first founder became "the difficult one," and people stopped listening to him. He told me, "I feel like my rights are taken away."

His cofounder thought he was protecting the team from harshness. The team learned that the founders weren't aligned, and one of them could be ignored.

People read body language and feel tension between others even when nobody names it.

In a meeting, they notice who interrupts whom, who questions whom and in what tone, and whether one founder has withdrawn. The more often the two of you fight, the louder those signals get. It shows up in the work. One of you hands someone a task. Then the other tells them it's the wrong priority, and the work gets redone.

Founders' moods carry extra weight. You hold status and power. People idealize you, mostly without realizing it. In my experience, many employees start to relate to a founder the way they once related to a parent or to whoever held power in their lives.

In Emotional Contagion (1994), Elaine Hatfield and colleagues described how emotions spread through groups. People pick up and mirror the feelings of those around them. Later work on teams by Thomas Sy and others (2005) found that a leader's mood spreads to the group and affects how well the group coordinates. When two founders are tense in a meeting, the room tends to stay tense after they leave.

Think about children whose parents are fighting. The kids often don't know what the fight is about, and they feel it anyway. They notice the tone at dinner and the door that shuts a little too hard. They can't fix it and they can't leave, because they depend on both parents.

So they adapt. Some drift toward anxiety and some act out. Others take a side, try to become the peacemaker, or shut down. A team is in a similar spot. Their paychecks and much of their identity are tied to the two of you. And they have far less control over the company's future than you do.

When people can't fix the tension above them, many seek connection to whichever founder keeps them safest.

Say the CEO has been hinting that the CTO is underperforming. If I'm an employee, it makes sense to get closer to the CEO, because she holds more power. I'll keep feeding her information and try to learn how she thinks. I'll keep the CTO happy on the surface, but stop giving him honest feedback.

The psychiatrist Murray Bowen, in the family systems theory he developed from the 1950s through the 1970s, called this triangulation. When tension between two people gets too high, a third person gets pulled in to absorb some of it. That takes attention off the original conflict, so the conflict between the two founders stays frozen.

I often think about the people who often get pulled in to mediate conflict between founders as parentified employees—the emotionally intelligent individuals wired for caretaking. They often end up in Head of People, HR, or Chief of Staff roles. Being the go-between can feel good at first. It tells an employee, "I'm valued here. I'm important." It also pulls their attention away from their own work, and tends to raise their anxiety.

Founders can feed this dynamic without noticing. An employee comes to you frustrated with your cofounder. You're frustrated with him too, so you sigh, agree and maybe add a story of your own. This provides temporary relief from the tension and helps you and the employee feel closer, but it prevents your cofounder from hearing the friction necessary for change. Icing him out reinforces the narrative that he is not to be respected, and accelerates the chances of his eventual departure. What would be far more helpful is coaching the employee to take the feedback to your cofounder directly.

Startup Snapshot studied startup employee wellbeing. Employees whose founder was highly stressed reported 14% higher burnout. Cofounder conflict disrupts your ability to focus and execute, and negatively impacts your employees. The longer you fight, the higher the risk of churn your company faces.

Get realigned with your cofounder before you try to fix anything on the team. With the pair above, I started by bringing attention to the word that kept causing damage. I asked them to define micromanagement together and to stop using it as a weapon in front of the team. Then, I suggested they increase their frequency of operational syncs so they could enter meetings fully aligned.

After you've made initial progress with your cofounder, show the team the culture you want. Your team copies what you do, so let them see you disagree, work it out, and commit to a decision. Because of the power gap, that alone won't give most employees the same freedom to push back. So ask for it directly, and when it comes, handle it well.

The next time someone vents to you about your cofounder, ask whether they've told your cofounder directly, and help them figure out how they could. That small shift can help contain conflict so it doesn't contaminate your execution.

Bowen, M. (1978). Family therapy in clinical practice. Jason Aronson.

Hatfield, E., Cacioppo, J. T., & Rapson, R. L. (1994). Emotional contagion. Cambridge University Press.

Startup Snapshot. (n.d.). Employee wellbeing. Retrieved November 5, 2026, from https://www.startupsnapshot.com/research/employee-wellbeing/

Sy, T., Côté, S., & Saavedra, R. (2005). The contagious leader: Impact of the leader's mood on the mood of group members, group affective tone, and group processes. Journal of Applied Psychology, 90(2), 295–305. https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.90.2.295

#4776. Send your name to Saturn’s largest moon

Published Oct 30, 2026 2:34 PM EDT

NASA is still on track to send its Dragonfly rotocraft to Saturn’s moon Titan by the end of the decade, and you can come along for the ride. Well, you can at least add your initials to the flight roster.

As part of its Journey to Titan campaign, NASA has opened an online registry that will be included on a microchip aboard the spacecraft when it launches. The launch is currently scheduled for no earlier than July 2028. Signees will receive a personalized digital “boarding pass,” as proof that their names will reach the ice-encased Saturnian moon in 2034. While the encoded autographs may not do much to help with the overall mission, it’s nice to know that you will be represented on what may become one of the most consequential space endeavors of all time.

“We are excited to bring humanity along for the journey of a lifetime, and we invite everyone to send their names on this small, but mighty rotorcraft that will unlock the secrets of the universe,” Nicky Fox, NASA’s Science Mission Directorate associate administrator, said in the announcement.

Titan is the largest of Saturn’s 292 known moons, and a longtime dream destination in the search for life beyond Earth. Although Titan features dusty dunes overlooking lakes and rivers of methane, the frigid surface also maintains a temperature of around −290 degrees Fahrenheit. This is inhospitable to life as we know it, but a giant ocean also exists beneath the icy shell. Astrobiologists widely agree that these waters probably contain enough complex compounds to facilitate a prebiotic environment. Laboratory simulations of Titan’s atmosphere have also indicated its gaseous conditions can even form some of the principle building blocks for DNA and RNA. If true, extraterrestrial microbial life may exist within the moon’s hidden waters.

However, there’s no way to confirm the possibility without directly examining Titan’s conditions. That’s where Dragonfly comes into play. After over six years of interplanetary travel, NASA’s eight-bladed robotic rotocraft will land on the moon and begin its environmental survey. Dragonfly’s vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) capabilities will allow it to travel to multiple locations over the planned three-year mission. If all goes well, the rotocraft will journey across 70 miles on Titan, while visiting 20 to 30 different areas.

“By flying the first-ever rotorcraft science mission, NASA will…we search for signs of habitability on a distant world that is most similar to our own,” added Fox.

Dragonfly is currently under construction at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland. It marks the fourth mission in NASA’s New Frontiers Program, which is dedicated to further exploration of the planets and moons that comprise our solar system.

Adding your name to Dragonfly’s log is likely a no-brainer for many people, but there is no rush if you need to take some time to ponder the decision. Signees have until 11:59 p.m. EST on January 15, 2027, to make their (digital) mark.

#4775. Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine said.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine said.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

The lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine said.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also important to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he said.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he said.

Trinh said he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh said.

#4774. Tesla drops car referral rewards, now pays owners in FSD for referrals

Tesla has launched a new referral program in the US that pays owners in Full Self-Driving (Supervised) instead of rewarding car sales. A referred owner gets one free month of FSD, and the referrer gets a free month or a $99 Tesla Credit if that person starts paying.

At the same time, Tesla’s Refer and Earn terms no longer list any vehicle as a qualifying purchase for buyer or referrer rewards. Buy a Tesla with a friend’s code today and neither of you gets anything.

To share a link, you need to be paying for FSD (Supervised) monthly or own it outright from before Tesla stopped selling it, according to Tesla’s FSD referral support page. Owners who got FSD through a one-year grant can’t participate. The link lives under “Refer and Earn” in the Tesla app, version 4.62.0 or later.

The person on the other end has to own a registered Tesla with compatible hardware, can’t have paid for FSD in the past 12 months, and can’t have bought it outright. There’s also a catch for recent buyers: anyone who got a free FSD trial with a new car is locked out of referral links until 12 months after that trial ends.

The bigger change is buried in Tesla’s Refer and Earn page. Buyer benefits now apply to solar panels only. Referrer benefits cover solar, first demo drives (up to 30 over an account’s lifetime) and the new FSD referral.

Model 3, Model Y and Cybertruck only show up under loyalty benefits, for existing owners buying another Tesla product. Model S and Model X aren’t listed at all.

Tesla didn’t announce the change. The page is stamped “Updated February 24, 2026,” so it’s unclear exactly when vehicles came off the list.

That’s quite a turn for a program that was always about moving cars. When Tesla brought the referral program back in August 2024, a buyer got $1,000 off a Model S, X, Y or 3, and the referrer got $500 in credit. Tesla has killed and revived the program several times over the past decade, but cars were always at the center of it. Not anymore.

That’s the exact metric in Elon Musk’s 2025 CEO Performance Award, which includes a milestone of 10 million active FSD subscriptions. It’s the reason Tesla started disclosing the number in January in the first place.

The free month a friend receives doesn’t count toward that total. A paid conversion does, and that’s precisely the event the new program pays for.

The only way I would ever pay for FSD is if Tesla covered full comprehensive insurance for my vehicle and accepted all liability. Otherwise, it's a gamble with my (and others') life.

That they seem to prioritize this sham service (Just call it Assisted Driving for honesty sake?) versus improving the cars or lowering prices, tells me enough not to look at Tesla for my next vehicle.

The recipient has to already own a Tesla, so the program doesn’t add a single car to the fleet. It’s built to mine the existing fleet for subscriptions. Tesla had sold about 8.9 million vehicles by the end of 2025, and only 1.74 million are paying for FSD, so there’s plenty of room. At Q3’s pace, we estimated 10 million subscriptions is still about eight years away.

So Tesla stopped paying for referrals that require selling a car, and started paying for the ones that move the number in Musk’s pay package. We think that tells you a lot about where the company’s priorities are right now.

#4773. Psychedelic nasal spray treats depression with toad-inspired goo

Published Oct 30, 2026 3:45 PM EDT

A powerful psychedelic compound best associated with the Sonoran desert toad (Incilius alvarius) has been recreated in a lab and transformed into a fast-acting nasal spray. A recent clinical trial outlined this week in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) suggests this spray could help people with treatment resistant depression, without the often less pleasant element of psychedelics. In the study, a single squeeze of the spray eased patients’ depressive symptoms with benefits lasting throughout the eight week trial.

Crucially, those long-term benefits (which have also been observed in other psychedelic research) didn’t require enduring an all-day mystical trip. Most patients were cleared for release less than two hours after taking the spray. Thankfully, the approach also eliminates the need to fondle a toxic amphibian. That’s potentially a plus both for patients and overharvested toad populations. The finds come amid a resurgence in new research and investment involving psychedelics, supported in part by evolving political attitudes towards the compounds on federal and state levels.

The nasal spray was developed by biotech firm AtaiBeckley. Its  active ingredient is called mebufotenin, which is also known as 5-MeO-DMT. The compound occurs naturally in several places, but it is most famously associated with the secretions of the Sonoran desert toad. For decades, amateur psychonauts have sought out these meaty North American toads for the prominent glands located on the amphibian’s head and hind legs. Squeezing those glands releases a milky secretion (sometimes inaccuracy referred to as venom), which when dried and then vaporized, produces an intense psychedelic experience. Many people who have smoked it describe a profound sense of oneness or ego dissolution, and some even report the sensation of dying.

Though based on the same compound, the drug in the nasal spray is synthetic and made in a lab. The researchers wanted to see if a controlled, clinical dose of 5-MeO-DMT could deliver some of the compound’s reported therapeutic benefits while keeping the overall treatment brief, especially compared with longer-acting psychedelics like psilocybin. They  limited their study to 193 adults between the ages of 18 to 75 with treatment-resistant depression. The participants, who came from the United States, Europe, and Australia, had each already tried at least two antidepressant treatments without success. By some estimates, around a third of all patients experiencing major depressive disorder also have treatment resistant depression.

Each participant received nasal spray in either a low (.3mg), medium (8mg), or high (12mg) dose. Neither the patient, nor the clinical staff or researchers involved knew which dose was given. The most intense psychedelic effects wore off relatively quickly, regardless of the dose. Clinicians checked on the patients at regular intervals to determine if they were deemed safe enough to leave the clinic. Among participants who received the 8-milligram dose, 85 percent were ready for discharge within two hours, compared with 78 percent of those who received the 12-milligram dose.

However, the therapeutic effects of the spray appeared to persist far longer.  Patients who received the medium or high dose showed significantly greater improvement than the comparison group as early as two days after treatment, and that advantage held through the end of the eight-week study. The team measured depression with a clinical scale measuring from 0 to 60, with  higher scores indicating more severe symptoms. After four weeks, the 12 mg group had dropped an average of 11.1 points on that score. The 8mg group dropped an even higher 12.5 points while the .3mg group dropped 5.5 points. These findings suggest the nasal spray application could provide some of the same therapeutic effects of other scheduled therapies less less need to have healthcare workers monitoring patients for many hours at a time.

“In adults with treatment-resistant depression, single doses of intranasal mebufotenin benzoate were well tolerated and produced rapid, robust, and durable reductions in depressive symptoms,” the study authors write. “Intranasal mebufotenin benzoate may improve treatment access and convenience, requiring a shorter monitoring period and fewer clinic visits compared with psilocybin and esketamine, respectively.”

This experimental nasal spray arrives amid a transitionary period for psychedelic research. State governments have shown more interest in the field in recent years, with Oregon and Colorado each launching their own psilocybin programs. Even Texas, a state traditionally associated with a tough on drugs approach, just committed $50 million to research the powerful psychedelic ibogaine. Signs of movement are occurring at the federal level as well. In April, President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at accelerating research and FDA approval of psychedelic-based therapies.

Though it attracted significant attention, the executive order is really more signaling than action. It notably does not lower the bar a therapeutic needs to reach before archived FDA approval.

Still, pharmaceutical companies are clearly taking note. Earlier this year, Eli Lilly, the largest pharmaceutical company in the world, acquired AtariBeckley for $2.8 billion. AtaiBeckley developed the nasal spray used in the recent JAMA study.

#4772. Dog Training Methods: Many More Reasons to Use Rewards

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

The conversation about dog training methods feels like it’s been going on for a long time. It’s an important one to keep having because of the benefits to dogs and their humans when reward-based methods are used, and the risks if they’re not. One of the things that has changed over the years is that the list of reasons to recommend reward-based methods has gotten longer. Changing cultural attitudes towards pets also play a role. Below are some of the factors that explain why training your dog with rewards—such as food treats or play—is the way to go.

Reward-based methods work, which means there is no need to use aversive methods like leash jerks and prong collars. Several studies have found that dogs trained with reward-based methods are more obedient than those trained with aversives (e.g., Rooney & Cowan, 2011). One reason could be that stress from the use of aversives makes it harder for dogs to learn. Meanwhile, aversive methods have risks that include fear, anxiety, stress, and a worse relationship with their guardian (Casey et al., 2021; Vieira de Castro et al., 2019; Ziv, 2017). As anyone with a fearful or reactive dog knows, having a dog with behavior issues can be difficult and expensive; there is simply no point in using methods that risk making such behavior issues worse.

In the past, some people would make an argument—now known to be out-dated—that there were cases in which aversive methods might be used as a “last resort.” However, any time aversive methods are used, there are those risks to the dog’s welfare. And aversives are never needed as a “last resort” because reward-based methods work. Unfortunately, because dog training is not regulated, there are still some trainers who use aversive methods. Dog trainers who feel they need to use aversives should refer those cases to their reward-based colleagues while they update and improve their training skills.

These days, we recognize dogs as sentient beings. Dogs perceive the environment around them and they have feelings about it. That includes feelings about us. If people use aversive methods (like tugs on the leash, or loud noises to stop them doing something), the dog is going to have feelings about that and may even become afraid of the person who does this to them.

We used to think about animal welfare as being mainly about preventing cruelty. But now that we know animals are sentient, there’s been a shift in how we think about welfare. While preventing cruelty is still essential, good welfare also means providing positive experiences. Training your dog with positive reinforcement is one such good experience. Walks, play, toys, sniffing, and other types of enrichment are also positive experiences for your dog.

Our views on dog training have also changed. Training is about how to help the dog fit into our world and feel comfortable in it. Dogs aren’t born knowing how to behave around humans, so there is plenty that we need to teach them (including during the all-important socialization phase for puppies). But it’s also essential to ask if they are comfortable in a particular situation (like at the vet), and if not, how we can help them? It's also important to ask whether we are meeting their needs, like their need to play, to sniff, and to have companionship. This broader lens means we can do a much better job of helping dogs be happy, which is what everyone wants for their dog (Todd, 2020). And, in turn, it reduces the likelihood of behavior issues in the first place.

These days, we know that some dog behavior issues are due to pain or another medical issue (Mills et al., 2020). For example, if a dog doesn’t want to jump in the car at the end of a walk, reacts badly when you reach out to touch them, or has suddenly become terrified of fireworks (when they weren’t before), that could be due to a medical issue (Todd, 2024). If someone takes a punitive approach to training and merely tries to stop the behavior, it means that needed medical care is not happening and the dog’s suffering is compounded.

These days, good dog trainers are used to working with vets. They may suggest that a dog guardian sees their vet to investigate if there are any medical issues. As well, in some cases, veterinarians may recommend the use of psychoactive medications. Sometimes, it takes a team to help you with your dog’s behavior!

Cultural changes in how we view dogs mean that, these days, they’re our family members. When we see dogs as family, we see aversive methods differently too. The idea of applying sharp prongs to a dog’s neck or giving the dog an electric shock no longer seems just misguided, but also mean. Many people wonder, why would you do that to a family member who you profess to love? Often, dog guardians tell me it is a relief to learn that these methods are not needed, and that kind, humane methods work to train dogs and deal with behavior issues.

Professional organizations around the world recommend reward-based methods, and have been doing so for a long time (e.g., AVSAB, 2021; ACVB). Over the years, they have updated and rewritten their position statements to make it even clearer that reward-based methods are the best way to train your dog. If you have been using aversive methods, such as tugs on the leash, the good news is that you can switch over to reward-based methods right away. If you need help with your dog’s behavior, don’t be embarrassed to reach out for help—that’s what professionals are there for. See a reward-based dog trainer and/or your veterinarian, as appropriate, to get started.

#4769. Sir Patrick Stewart Dies at 86 After Battle With Alzheimer's, Lewy Body Dementia

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

#4766. What Does an Attention Deficit Really Mean?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Most of us have experienced what it’s like to struggle to pay attention to something. I’ll offer a recent example of my own.

My mind wandered further and further from the focus of the long academic meeting I was attending. I looked around at the others in the room. They seemed to be listening—or at least staring at the screen.

We were in a plush venue just off campus, the sort we often hire for these long meetings. Rain pounded on the glass roof. Beyond it, the grounds were lush and green.

A young waiter, about the same age as my son, clinked some glasses, replenished the water, juice and coffee, and left a tray of small chocolate brownies and fresh fruit at the back of the room.

I remember how I wanted one of the brownies and some plump green grapes, still shining with moisture. But walking to the back and helping myself felt rude. Everyone else seemed to be managing to pay attention. Weren’t they?

It felt as though I had lost all ability to focus.

But my attention hadn’t disappeared. I could focus on the rain, the trees, the grapes and the brownies. I could attend to them effortlessly. But I couldn’t keep my mind on the sixth presentation of the day.

I tried to care about what was being said. I really wanted to. But I simply couldn’t.

Something inside me had stopped cooperating. I’d reached a point of attentional saturation. It was a little like realising you’re full and that each extra mouthful feels forced.

I longed to get up, walk outside, or breathe fresh air. I wanted to think about something other than the presentation. I felt as though I was dying of boredom.

I felt resentful that I was expected to keep listening, but also guilty that I couldn’t find the attention the speaker seemed to deserve. What was wrong with me? Why was I so inconsiderate?

Perhaps you can remember similar experiences. Encountering situations in which our capacity to ‘pay attention’ is stretched is so often part of modern life.

I wondered what it reflected about me. Was I bored? Had the subject failed to interest me or feel important enough? Was it about motivation? Was I tired? Had I simply reached the limit of what I could sustain that day? Or was I reacting to an expectation that I should or must keep listening?

The idea that something can be ‘wrong’ with our ‘attention’ is now woven into the cultures and institutions in which we live. But psychologists don’t really use the term attention to describe one clearly defined ability.

In a 2019 paper, psychologists Bernhard Hommel and colleagues describe the common idea of attention as the mechanisms that help us make efficient use of our limited capacity to process, store and retrieve information. That sounds straightforward.

But the word is used as a proxy for a wide range of abilities and experiences:

These are all capacities that might be (and often are) referred to when someone uses the word ‘attention.’ However, Hommel and colleagues argue that it is highly unlikely that the same set of functional or neural mechanisms would be involved in and responsible for each of these. They also caution that dividing attention into neat, separate functions can obscure what those functions have in common too.

They’re all examples of "attention," but they might not share the same underpinning anatomical or neurological roots. This matters more than you might think. Their argument has implications beyond the lab.

For example, if attention describes different things, what are we saying when we tell someone to “pay attention”? Furthermore, what are we referring to when we say that someone has an “attention deficit”?

What’s more, when someone struggles to stay with a task, the difficulty may indeed involve attention. But it may also involve motivation, intention or emotion. Perhaps the task feels pointless, the person doesn’t want to do it, or they are bored. The label 'attention' alone doesn’t tell us which of these is at play in a situation.

Psychological labels deserve care and scrutiny, no matter how deeply entrenched they might be. A label can help us recognise a pattern. But it can frequently give us the impression that we understand more than we do.

The authors of the paper above ultimately concluded that we’d be better to drop the term 'attention' as a label for a specific functional or neural system, because, they argue, it doesn’t actually identify a single functional or neural system. This is significant.

If attention were no longer treated as the label for a single mental or neural system, what would we make of things like Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)? The name itself seems to point to a deficit in a particular capacity we call 'attention.' But if there is no single system called attention, then what, precisely, is deficient in something like ADHD?

This doesn’t necessarily make ADHD imaginary, or the difficulties people experience less real. But it does make the label seem less like an explanation than it first appears. Perhaps it names a recognisable pattern of difficulty, while leaving the processes, circumstances and histories that give rise to it in any one person wide open.

Hommel, B., Chapman, C. S., Cisek, P., Neyedli, H. F., Song, J. H., & Welsh, T. N. (2019). No one knows what attention is. Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 81 (7), 2288-2303.

#4765. Obesity in Your 20s and 30s May Increase Cancer Risk Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Younger adults with obesity may be more likely to develop cancer before midlife than those who maintain a moderate weight, according to a study published on October 26 in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

The risk for cancer became higher as weight increased. The highest rates were seen in those with severe obesity and abdominal obesity.

This highlights the potential importance of weight management in the prevention of early onset cancer.

Rates of both obesity and early onset cancer are rising among younger adults globally.

This study analyzed data from the Korean National Health Insurance Service database. The researchers identified 6,313,338 adults ages 20 to 39 who had no history of cancer and who underwent standardized national health screenings.

The researchers followed the participants for an average of 11 years.

Body mass index (BMI) was categorized into five groups ranging from underweight to class II obesity using the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria for Asian populations. Waist circumference was also measured as an indicator of abdominal adiposity.

During the analysis, the researchers adjusted for various factors such as:

Over the follow-up period, there were 151,893 cases of cancer among the participants. The incidence rate increased progressively based on obesity categories, from 1.84% in “normal-weight” individuals to 2.24% in class I obesity and 2.62% in class II obesity.

The strongest associations were seen in the following cancers:

Obesity was not associated with breast cancer diagnosed before the age of 50.

Ketan Thanki, MD, board certified colorectal surgeon with the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in Long Beach, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained to Healthline that obesity itself causes states that promote cancer formation.

This current study focused on the Korean population. However, the connection between obesity and cancer risk is a global issue.

Previous research has shown that around 10% of all new cancer diagnoses in the United States are associated with obesity. Obesity also accounts for up to 50% of certain cancers, including endometrial and liver cancer.

The study also showed that waist circumference, which indicates abdominal obesity, may be linked to cancer risk that is similar to that of individuals with overweight.

The study researchers used the thresholds set out by the Korean Society for the Study of Obesity. These thresholds put the waist circumference cutoff at over 90 cm (35.4 in) for males and over 85cm (33.46 in) for females.

These are not universal cutoffs. According to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), waist circumference measurements that can increase your risk of negative health issues are 101.6 cm (40 in) for males and 88.9 cm (35 in) for females.

Previous research has also suggested an association between waist circumference and cancer risk, independent of BMI. One study showed a potential 11% increased risk of cancer in people with a waist circumference over the thresholds, even if they were physically active.

The current study found that males had a higher relative association between obesity and cancer, while females showed higher absolute risk.

The researchers also found that the absolute risk was higher in adults ages 30 to 39.

Those who currently smoke or who have ever smoked were also found to have a higher risk of developing cancer than those who have never smoked.

“Diet, exercise, and now medications can all be used very effectively to reduce one’s weight and, hopefully as a result, cancer risk,” Thanki said.

He also noted that, due to differences between South Korean populations and those in other countries such as the United States, further studies will be needed to determine how this translates across other populations.

“But I think this trend will likely extend across all cultures,” he said.
