#4749. How Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) Can Help With Trauma

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) is an evidence-based treatment rooted in cognitive behavioral therapy and designed to treat PTSD and trauma from combat, childhood sexual abuse, sexual assault, rape, abuse, and life-altering experiences. CPT focuses on how traumatic events create distorted beliefs, and how subsequent behaviors, influenced by those beliefs, develop as a way to protect you from future harm while effectively cutting you off from life, connection, and love.

We all have beliefs about the world, ourselves, and others. When a shocking, upsetting, or threatening event happens, we try to make sense of it, and that can lead us to change our beliefs and adopt distorted thoughts. Distorted thoughts generally follow one of two unhelpful paths:

Assimilation: This is when you change the facts about the trauma to maintain an old belief. An example of assimilation is thinking, "I was assaulted because I stayed out too late." Instead of putting responsibility where it belongs, on the perpetrator, you blame yourself. Why? Because self-blame allows you to maintain beliefs about fairness and gives you the false sense that you can keep yourself safe if you just follow the rules.

Overaccommodation: In this case, you change your beliefs to extreme degrees to protect yourself from ever getting hurt again. An example of overaccommodation is thinking, "All men are evil and cannot be trusted," or "I am permanently broken."

In CPT, these rigid thoughts are called stuck points. They keep you trapped in survival mode and prevent you from fully healing and moving past the trauma.

Once a stuck point takes hold, trauma survivors begin to rely on avoidance to cope. Avoidance is the number one coping mechanism for human beings, but for a trauma survivor, it is their main strategy. If you are a trauma survivor, you avoid places, people, conversations, intimacy, thoughts, and internal sensations that remind you of the event.

Avoidance makes sense. It offers quick, short-term relief and tricks you into believing you are in control. The truth is quite the opposite. Avoidance strengthens the stuck point, reinforces fear, and makes recovery nearly impossible. Its function is to protect you from danger, but it also pushes away genuine love, support, and connection.

CPT gives you a structured and effective way to face what you have been avoiding without getting you too overwhelmed or requiring you to retell every detail of your trauma. Fear of reliving the event is one of the main reasons many people avoid getting treatment in the first place. Working collaboratively with a trained clinician, you learn how to identify your stuck points, examine the evidence for and against them, test their validity and helpfulness, and choose healthier, more adaptive behaviors instead of avoidance.

CPT is a short-term modality, usually completed in 12 to 16 structured sessions, and it works powerfully in both individual and group settings. It helps you explore stuck points across five core areas of well-being: safety, trust, power and control, esteem, and intimacy. In my 25-plus years of clinical experience, and especially in my work with women survivors of childhood sexual abuse and adult sexual assault, I have seen firsthand how transformative this process is.

Trauma carries with it a host of lies. It lies about who you are, it lies about your worth, and it lies about what you deserve. Facing trauma takes real courage, but you do not have to live your life running away from fear. You deserve peace. You deserve joy. And you are worthy of love. CPT gives you the tools to truly see the lies trauma creates, helps you reclaim your power, and opens your heart again.

#4748. Fierce turtles square off in a rare woodland turf battle

Published Nov 1, 2026 10:10 AM EST

At first, it appears that two turtles with yellow spots are calmly sitting side by side. Suddenly, one of them turns, slowly—and lunges out with its head, its open beak clearly trying to take an aggressive chomp out of its neighbor. Moments later, the turtle tries again. Now, both reptiles are going head-to-head, though each is retracted into the protection of its shell.

The two combatants are male eastern box turtles (Terrapene carolina carolina) competing for dominance. Eastern box turtles are a subspecies of the common box turtle (Terrapene carolina), with bright orange and yellow coloring on its dark shell. They live throughout the eastern and midwestern United States.

“I wouldn’t say that they’re normally aggressive, but male box turtles can definitely become territorial, especially since males’ home ranges (the area they frequently occupy) often overlap,” Eamon Caffrey, the turtle research coordinator at Mass Audubon who captured the video, tells Popular Science. “We do occasionally see this sort of brawling behavior between two males when out in the field; you just have to get lucky enough to actually witness it. This experience was a first for me, and I was thrilled to capture it on camera.”

Over the summer, another Mass Audubon staff member saw two male box turtles opting for a pushing contest instead of biting. At one point, one of the two flipped the other contestant onto its back and pushed him down a small hill. Box turtle battles can also feature spinning each other around.

“From my understanding, fights between male box turtles are much more opportunistic than anything else,” Caffrey tells Popular Science. “Often, when two males come in contact, they will display a variety of aggressive behaviors that can include head butting, shell ramming, biting, pushing, and shoving – all in attempts to assert dominance. These disputes are often territorial but can be over mates as well.”

What’s more, the turtle with the darker shell is a well-known individual over 30 years old. Caffrey says he’s seen him various times this year, and since capturing the video the celebrity reptile has been spending time in an area where the Mass Audubon team frequently spot two to three adult females. However, there’s been no trace of his opponent.

“Does that mean he ‘won’ the battle?” Caffrey muses. “Who knows.”

#4747. Yes, electric motorcycles will replace gasoline motorcycles, but not the way you think

For years, the conventional wisdom surrounding electric motorcycles has been fairly straightforward: Build an electric motorcycle that’s just as good as a gasoline-powered motorcycle, make it affordable enough, and eventually riders will switch.

It’s essentially the same playbook that electric cars have followed. Make the electric version competitive enough, and eventually the market will move in that direction.

But I think we’ve been looking at electric motorcycles all wrong. Because the future of electric motorcycles isn’t necessarily about convincing today’s gasoline motorcycle riders to switch. It’s about the next generation of riders who won’t have any reason to start with gasoline in the first place.

And that’s a much bigger deal than it might sound. In fact, it’s the entire key to the puzzle. Because make no mistake, the future of motorcycling is electric. It just won’t happen the way most people think.

The problem with applying the electric car playbook to motorcycles is that motorcycles aren’t cars.

For most people, a car is a tool. It’s transportation. Sure, some drivers are deeply passionate about their cars, but they are a minority. The vast majority simply want something comfortable, reliable, affordable, and convenient to get them from point A to point B.

Motorcycles, especially in markets like the US and Europe, are different. In fact, it’s the complete opposite of the car situation. For a minority of Western riders, and especially American riders, a motorcycle is a tool. For the vast majority, it’s a passion. People generally buy motorcycles because they love motorcycles. And for many riders, that love is deeply intertwined with the gasoline engine itself.

The sound, the vibration, the shifting, the mechanical character. These aren’t necessarily flaws to be engineered away. They’re part of the experience for traditional riders.

You can show someone like that an electric motorcycle with better acceleration, lower maintenance costs, cheaper operating expenses, and the convenience of charging at home, and they still won’t want it.

Not because the electric motorcycle isn’t good enough, but because it isn’t what they love.

And that’s fine. There’s nothing wrong with loving gasoline motorcycles if that’s your thing. But it means that trying to convert those riders may be a losing battle, at least on any meaningful timeline.

Unfortunately though, it seems many years were wasted on that approach. Take Harley-Davidson, for example.

The brand started building its first electric motorcycle over a decade ago – commendable among all the other legacy motorcycle manufacturers that turned their noses up at the thought of going electric. When it was released in 2018, the Harley-Davidson LiveWire received rave reviews, but it just didn’t sell well. For one, it was insanely expensive at $30,000. But the other major reason was that no matter how amazing it was, it wasn’t going to scratch that gasoline itch that most riders still had.

That motorcycle still exists in small-scale production as the LiveWire One through H-D’s electric spinoff, but now LiveWire has wisened up to the real pathway to moving higher numbers of electric motorcycles with its S4 Honcho line. And this brings us to how electric motorcycles will really replace their gasoline counterparts.

Now consider what’s happening with younger riders today.

Millions of people are growing up riding electric bicycles, electric scooters, and increasingly powerful e-motos. For them, electric two-wheelers aren’t some strange new alternative to the real thing. They are the real thing.

They’ve grown accustomed to instant torque, quiet operation, and the simplicity of twisting a throttle and going. To these riders, a gasoline-powered motorcycle is laughably primitive. It’d be like me handing you a gasoline-powered drill or blender. Yeah, exactly. Now look who’s suddenly on team battery, eh?

So now we have a whole new generation of riders getting ready to come of age. And eventually, many of those riders are going to want something more.

Maybe they’ve spent years riding a 28 mph electric bike, or a 40 mph electric moto. Now they’re young adults, they want to ride on faster roads, and they want something capable of 70 or 80 mph that’s actually street legal. They’ve gone from a sixteen-year-old in a hoodie to a twenty-six-year-old in a collared shirt. Instead of getting to high school, now they’re getting to work. But they haven’t lost that desire to ride.

It’s not because they’ve carefully compared electric and gasoline motorcycles and decided that electric is superior. It’s not because they’re trying to save the planet or reduce their maintenance costs. It’s simply because they grew up with electric two-wheelers as the norm.

It’s simply the next logical step in the type of riding they’ve already been doing for years.

Will a few of them transition over to gasoline-powered motorcycles? Sure. But for most, gasoline motorcycles will never even enter the equation.

Don’t get me wrong, we haven’t seen the last of gasoline motorcycles.

And I don’t even think electric motorcycles are going to suddenly outsell gasoline motorcycles because they become objectively better machines. At least not in the traditional recreational motorcycle markets we’re talking about here.

Instead, I think we’re going to see a somewhat more gradual generational transition.

Today’s gasoline motorcycle enthusiasts will largely keep riding gasoline motorcycles. They’ll keep buying them, maintaining them, and enjoying them for as long as they can.

But as those riders age out of motorcycling, the next generation won’t replace them with another generation of gasoline motorcycle buyers. In other words, gasoline motorcycles will die out with their riders.

Increasingly, those younger riders will have already entered the world of powered two-wheelers through electric bikes and e-motos. When they’re ready to move up, electric motorcycles will be waiting for them.

And over those next few years, the technology will only become better. The only remaining Achilles’ heel of electric motorcycles – their run time – will get better and better as battery technology improves and we move towards solid-state batteries.

Suddenly they’ll be on par with gasoline motorcycles for range and ‘fueling’ time, yet will beat those combustion bikes elsewhere. But at that point, “better” won’t even matter anymore as electrics will be the only comfortable option for the vast majority of new riders. Again, you wouldn’t buy a power drill that runs on a gasoline engine when you’ve seen how convenient and effective a lithium-ion power drill has been your whole life.

Over time, the traditional gasoline motorcycle market will simply shrink as its existing customer base gets older, while electric motorcycles build an entirely new customer base alongside it.

And again, there will be exceptions in both directions. Some lifelong gasoline riders will enthusiastically embrace electric motorcycles, and some younger riders will still discover the appeal of combustion engines and running through the gears.

Living in SE Asia this all sounds very strange. The vast majority of the worlds bikes are not owned as toys, they are the main form of transport for the family. I agree with a lot of the article but Asia is already years ahead. The fuel shortages and sky high prices are pushing people electric far faster than riders are "aging out"

But the broader trend will be driven less by conversion and more by generational replacement.

That’s why electric motorcycles will eventually become the standard, even if they never manage to convince most of today’s gasoline motorcycle enthusiasts to switch.

Gasoline motorcycles won’t necessarily disappear because electric motorcycles finally beat them at their own game. They’ll fade because the next generation of riders will be playing a different game entirely.

In other words, and to paraphrase T. S. Eliot, gasoline motorcycles won’t go out with a bang, but with a whimper.

#4746. Eli teases the launch of a much faster electric microcar

Eli Electric Vehicles is getting ready to reveal a new version of its tiny electric microcar, and this one could expand its usefulness beyond the slow lane.

In an Instagram teaser ahead of EICMA in Milan, the company announced the upcoming Eli ZERO MX, describing it as a new L7e vehicle joining its lineup. Eli also teased a special Race Edition, with promotional artwork showing a dark, sporty-looking ZERO with red accents and a visibly open-sided cabin.

The teaser doesn’t give us much to go on in terms of hard and fast details, but the L7e designation is the biggest clue here.

The familiar European Eli ZERO that we test-drove a few years ago is an L6e light quadricycle, with a top speed of 45 km/h (28 mph). Its compact two-seat layout makes it an appealing urban runabout, though that speed ceiling limits its usefulness on faster roads. But L7e vehicles can typically travel at speeds of up to 80-90 km/h (50-56 mph).

A faster version could make the little EV practical for considerably more trips. And there’s already a tantalizing hint: Eli’s Italian website lists an L7e ZERO capable of 85 km/h (53 mph), with a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles). Whether those specifications directly describe the upcoming ZERO MX remains unconfirmed by the teaser.

If they do, that would suggest a much more versatile commuter while retaining the tiny footprint that makes these vehicles so easy to park.

I like the idea of a faster LSV, maybe able to cruise at 40 mph. Not a good idea for freeways but suitable for almost all urban and suburban streets. For some a better option than a bike as an urban or second vehicle.

The Race Edition raises a different set of questions. The new vehicle could feature a sportier design, such as race seats and alternative doors. That could point toward a playful or more tuned vehicle, though we’ll have to wait to learn whether “Race” means additional performance or primarily a styling package.

It’s also unclear how closely the Race Edition and ZERO MX are related. The caption presents them separately, while the artwork additionally points towards a second-generation ZERO.

Either way, a roughly 50 mph Eli would be an interesting proposition: still small enough to rethink how much vehicle a daily commute requires, but potentially fast enough to cover routes the original couldn’t comfortably handle.

Eli says the reveal takes place at EICMA, November 3–8, in Hall 22, Stand B40. We’ll be there to see what they unveil.

#4745. How to build an air purifier in 6 simple steps

Published Nov 1, 2026 3:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

Though invisible itself, the air we breathe is a microcosm of identifiable pollen, fungal spores, viruses, dust particles, and fine particles of human pollution from everything from cars to asphalt sidewalks. It’s not something we should obsess over day to day, but as more people measure air quality on their own, many are getting readings they’d prefer to address. However, not everyone wants to buy an air purifier, which can cost several hundred dollars.

One proposed solution for at-home air filtration is to use readily available materials like cardboard, box fans, square HVAC filters, and everyone’s favorite building material: duct tape. I did a version of this myself for PopSci, and, though I have mixed feelings about the process, I’m overall satisfied with the result. Here, we’ll go through what I built, how I built it, and my overall conclusions after using it, along with resources for anyone interested in reading further.

There are several configurations for making your own air purifier at home. One of the most documented is a Corsi-Rosenthal box, or CR box for short. It’s essentially an air filter cube, which is what I’ll be calling mine, with four sides made of furnace filters and one side made of a standard box fan (seen above). The fan pulls air through the filters and pushes out cleaner air than came in.

The United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) provides a lot of information about DIY air cleaners, including visual construction guides, tips on improving DIY air cleaners, and general air cleaner usage advice. EPA research on DIY air cleaners for wildfire smoke will also inevitably interest those in wildfire-prone areas who don’t want to purchase an air purifier for smoke.

These resources were used extensively throughout this project. Instead of using this guide as a total replacement for these resources, use this page as a waypoint for how an individual or student group might use one of these devices, with practical concerns highlighted along the way.

I went to my local Walmart and bought a Lasko box fan, two pairs of Filtrete 20-inch MERV 11 furnace filters, and a roll of Duck Brand General Purpose Masking Tape. This represents what a typical consumer might buy without specialty ordering options or bulk purchasing. The total came to $73.58 before taxes and $78.36 after Florida state sales tax.

The box fan, or any fan in a roughly square housing, should be a modern ETL- or UL-listed fan (clearly marked on the box) because older fans and those not ETL- or UL-listed may have issues when run facing upward. This is a safety issue and should not be skipped.

Since the cardboard box your fan comes in will likely become part of your air filter cube, it’s worth getting one that isn’t damaged, though you can tape over small tears.

EPA guidance recommends MERV13 or equivalent filters for the best experience. The MERV scale indicates how much and what kinds of particles the device can filter. High-tier MERV filters can be costly, so I opted for MERV11 since I was able to get a fairly good deal (around $23) per two-pack of these panels, and the notable difference between MERV11 and MERV13 was that the latter can handle forest fire smoke particles, which is not an issue in my area.

You can assemble your air filter cube in less than an hour, even with one person. Rather than a strict job that requires exhaustive measuring and cutting, it’s more of an approximate job that relies on the magic of tape to do the heavy lifting. This is a feasible parent-and-child project for those 6+ and a solo project for those 10+.

For this project, we want air to flow in through the filters and out through the fan. That means that the part of the fan that blows air out needs to be on the exterior of your cube, and the back side of the fan that pulls in air needs to be on the inside of your cube. Like a surgeon marking which limb to operate on before making the first cut, I marked the interior of my fan with ‘I’s for safety. Meanwhile, your filters should have arrows. Those arrows should point towards the inside of the cube.

Place two filters together and use a small piece of tape to connect them as shown. Remember to have the arrows pointing inwards. Continue taping the filters until you form a square. You can either use two people here or secure one filter vertically with a trash bin to do it solo.

The resulting square will be flimsy and contain cracks that air can get through. Tape the seams with duct tape. Don’t worry about being imperfect on the first try. In fact, going over the seams multiple times will only make your cube more secure and airtight.

At this point, your square of filters should be feeling more and more structurally sound. You can now flip it over and repeat the simple taping method from Step 2 on the side that was previously on the ground.

Remember, the box is an important part of the final product. If you place your square over the box, you’ll see they’re roughly the same size. Carefully cut out the most structurally sound side of the box and trim it to be roughly the size of your filter square. It won’t need to be perfect. I used scissors for this, as if imitating a school project, but a standard box cutter or multitool with a cutting edge would be better.

When done, tape the cardboard to one end of your filter square. Your air filter cube now has a bottom.

As a last step, take the fan and put it on the top side of the box, taping it down carefully. If your fan has rounded corners, tape those too. If you notice small gaps in the fan housing, you can seal them with tape, provided they aren’t ventilation openings or near electrical components.

At this point, you have a completed air filter cube. With the fan side up, plug it into an outlet and turn the fan on. Look for structural integrity, a smooth spinning blade with no obstructions from tape or cardboard, and no unusual sounds or vibrations. I recommend being around your new filter cube for a bit before leaving it unattended. Follow any fan manufacturer guidance about long-term or unattended usage.

While I opted not to, you may optionally wish to cover the top of your air filter cube with the cardboard from the other side of the fan box, cutting out a circular hole over the spot where the blades spin. This reduces unintended air recirculation and overall increases the efficiency of the box.

Verdict: Making an air filter cube or CR box is a worthwhile experiment that results in a usable final product, but it may not be the best bang for your buck out there.

After having run my air filter cube for several days now, despite not currently being in possession of an air quality monitor, I can still tell it has worked. For example, there is visible dust on the outside of the filters, which accumulated while I was cleaning dusty gear nearby. Furthermore, neither the grill nor the fan blades themselves are showing the dust that typically accumulates on long-running fans. I would call this project, from an engineering perspective, an obvious success.

Functional mechanics aren’t the only issue, though. Money is time and time is money, and both of these are major issues with these boxes.

One of my biggest complaints about how CR boxes are described to the public is that they are “marketed” as cheap when filters are so expensive. Claims of hyper-cheap CR boxes with EPA-like performance are abundant, though EPA sources use MERV13. My use of MERV11, while reasonable, is another reason to call my creation an air filter cube rather than a true CR box.

Low-cost air purifiers are available commercially that even include HEPA filtration. For example, the Dreo Air Purifier for Home is just $44 right now and, according to Google Chrome’s Shopping Insights tool, despite its $100 MSRP, has never been above $56.

The Dreo air purifier highlights a lot of what feels absent from a DIY air filter cube: a small body you can comfortably place in your home, quiet operation, and filter changes that don’t require completely rebuilding the air purifier every time the filters are used up. For average consumers, I suspect something like the Dreo, or even a larger air purifier like the Levoit Core 300, is going to be a much better option in nearly every way.

Where this really shines is student science. Building your own air filtration cube is fun, sort of like Minecraft block crafting in real life. Students can explore airflow, cost-effectiveness of different materials, and bring home a usable appliance at the end of a one-hour lesson.

I particularly like the idea of students experimenting with different MERV levels, or comparing the effectiveness of low-cost commercial purifiers to their air filtration cubes. Students can, and should, ask themselves at what point the additional health benefits stop justifying the costs in time and money. These sorts of questions are at the core of environmental and healthcare policies that dictate our real world.

#4744. Losing Weight in Your 50s May Protect Your Heart Health Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to new research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, said Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

“By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she said.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz said the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

She said researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”

Weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he said. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

“It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy said.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy said. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

Wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, launched in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham said the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

The study showed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also said the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Cunningham said adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive plan,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

#4743. Should One Screen Out a Passion That Won't Work?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

In a previous post, I explored the idea of "limerence," or hopeless love for someone unattainable, as a negative force: the source of opportunity cost, stress, and even damage to one's health. But limerence can also be viewed as the inspiration for numerous immortal works of art explicitly based on such misguided passion.Any continued examination of the concept seems to reinforce the binary—sometimes good, sometimes bad—aspect of this concept. For example, while common sense might counsel avoiding any infatuation that seems to hold no hope of being reciprocated, let alone consummated, the implied desirability of censoring such impulses carries equally negative connotations.This is borne out by experience as well as research. After all, infatuation—in particular, emotional and erotic infatuation (sometimes known as a "crush")—by definition is triggered in an environment where information, whether positive or negative regarding future prospects, is insufficient or deliberately ignored. Constructing pre-emptive filters to censor such impulses could, it's true, break the kind of exploration that might result in hopeless attachment; but it might also euthanize an attraction which, once more information becomes available, looks to be more productive than first thought.Studies of individuals apt to self-censor feelings and thoughts show a strong correlation between self-censorship on the one hand, and insecurity and lack of self-esteem on the other. Logically, this implies that the confidence to not-censor thoughts and feelings is boosted by or enhances confidence in self. Clearly, self-confidence is a quality that allows an individual to explore and venture further, in relationships as in other fields. There's more on the positive side. Hopeless infatuations or crushes on others can act as a safety valve for people in otherwise committed relationships, adding a measure of thrill to daily life even as the impossibility of following through on the crush prevents the sort of life-damage an actual affair might entail. [1]But, as the student mentioned in my previous post found out, limerence can go too far, causing stress that may be emotionally and physically damaging, amid long-term behavior that has more in common with addiction than with healthy attachment.

In fact, a National Institutes of Health article collating research on links between love and addiction found conclusively that "drug addiction, on the one hand, and at least certain love-related experiences or behaviors, on the other, can reasonably be understood to be equivalent phenomena at the level of the brain, underwritten by the same neurophysiological processes." The article cites studies that posit the use of both therapy and chemical means, such as prescribing oxytocin and dopamine, to check the attachment process and break harmful love addiction: insisting at the same time that whether and how much harm is done must be the primary criterion in assessing if and how to interfere with limerence.The overall lesson of that article, and of this one, is that we must be careful when venturing into the territory of a strong, though hopeless, passion. "Love hurts," the band Nazareth sang; "Love is a drug," according to Roxie Music; "I can't make you love me," moaned Bonnie Raitt. When unrequited passion for someone starts to actively damage one's life, especially when it displays symptoms similar to addiction, research and experience show it should be looked into and treated if necessary. But would any of us want to live a life where passionate attachment was automatically screened out? Isn't passion, whether it works out or no, a fundamental characteristic of living life to the full?

[1] O’Sullivan, L. F., Belu, C. F., & Garcia, J. R. (2021). Loving you from afar: Attraction to others (“crushes”) among adults in exclusive relationships, communication, perceived outcomes, and expectations of future intimate involvement. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships. Advance online publication. DOI: 10.1177/02654075211038612

#4742. 2026 Gifts of the Year: Our editors have picked the best presents for anyone on your list

Updated Nov 1, 2026 3:42 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

A gift card isn’t a terrible present, but we believe you can do better. That’s why the editors here at Popular Science have put together this list of our favorite gifts of the year. We spend all year researching, testing, and covering products, so we know what we’re talking about. Even if you don’t end up grabbing one of these exact products, it’s a great place to start. Show them you know what they like and leave the gift cards for your nephew who you don’t really like that much.

Popular Science‘s sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at PCMag, CNET, Mashable, Lifehacker, and ZDNET.

Waterproof trail shoes usually look and feel too bulky and—let’s be honest—kind of nerdy. The Speedgoat 7 GTX keeps the regular Speedgoat 7’s supercritical EVA midsole and Vibram Megagrip outsole, then wraps them in a GORE-TEX Invisible Fit membrane and a recycled Cordura upper. It’s a lot of technical materials, but they’re wrapped in a design that actually looks cool with a pair of jeans. Toggle laces work with gloves on, there’s a loop for attaching gaiters (sold separately), and reflective details run all the way around for dark November runs. We recommend going up a half-size from your giftee’s typical number for a better fit.

This little device gives the gift of time that would otherwise be spent doomscrolling. Phone screen-time limits are easy to dismiss because the override button sits right under your thumb. Brick moves the override into another room. The $59 block has no battery, just an NFC chip. You pick the apps to lock in the free iPhone or Android app, tap your phone to the Brick, and those apps stay locked until you walk back and tap again. One Brick works with multiple phones, so a household can share it, and the app includes five emergency unlocks per device for real emergencies. It requires iOS 18 or Android 12 and later. Brick is also HSA and FSA eligible, which makes it a stocking stuffer you can buy with pretax money.

Insta360 made its name with 360-degree and action cameras, and the Luna Ultra is its first pocket gimbal camera, co-engineered with Leica. The main camera pairs a Leica Summicron lens with a 1-inch sensor that records up to 8K at 30fps, and a second telephoto camera on a 1/1.3-inch sensor handles zoomed shots and background blur. A three-axis gimbal keeps footage steady while you walk. The 2-inch OLED touchscreen pops off and works as a wireless monitor and remote, so you can frame a shot of yourself from across the room. It’s a serious content creation tool that’s fun to use, which is a rarity.

You don’t need a massive backyard to have a true outdoor pizza oven. The propane cooker weighs 26.4 pounds and measures 16.9 inches wide, yet Gozney rates it to reach 950 degrees Fahrenheit, which is more than enough to put a perfect char on a true Neopolitan style pie. Gozney’s lateral rolling flame wraps heat over the top of the pizza while a 12mm stone floor stores heat for the crust. An infrared thermometer makes a smart add-on gift, since the oven won’t tell you when the stone is ready. You’ll selfishly also probably get some free pizza out of it.

A 65-inch black rectangle is a lot of nothing to stare at when the TV is off. LG’s Gallery TV LX7B fills that space with art. The 4K Mini LED set has a matte screen that cuts reflections and a snow-white magnetic frame that snaps onto the bezel, and when it’s idle it can display pieces from LG Gallery+, a library of more than 5,000 works (some features require a Gallery+ subscription). It runs webOS 26 with Google Gemini built in. Whether the receiver is a film buff or a die-hard design enthusiast, this TV fits the bill.

This is a product we use every single day. The Theragun Mini Plus is Therabody’s smallest heated massage gun, and its attachment warms up to 131 degrees Fahrenheit across three heat levels. It has three speeds, two buttons, USB-C charging, and a travel lock that keeps it from switching on inside a gym bag. Therabody says heat plus percussion works three times faster than percussion alone, based on its own lab testing. You can run either therapy by itself, too. Don’t think this is only for hardcore gym rats. It’s great for people who just want to relax of even improve their sleep.

If you know a budding streamer or podcaster, this is a gift that grows with them. The Razer Seiren V3 Pro has both USB-C and XLR outputs, so it plugs straight into a PC now and into a mixer later when they upgrade their setup. It’s a dynamic mic with a 30mm cardioid capsule, a type that picks up less of a noisy room than most condensers. Onboard processing runs AI noise removal, a compressor, and a limiter on the mic itself, and Windows users can record 32-bit float audio through Razer Synapse. A tap-to-mute button, an RGB ring that shows mute and gain status, and an adjustable desk arm all come in the box.

The nightstand device, built for kids roughly 4 to 10, walks one child through morning, after-school, and bedtime routines a step at a time with visual prompts that work for kids who can’t read yet. It also handles alarm clock, sound machine, nightlight, and OK-to-wake duty. It has no camera or microphone, and kids can’t browse the web or download apps on it. Skylight sells it for $139.99, and the optional $39-per-year Buddy Plus plan adds rewards, timers, and read-aloud messages.

Fast wireless charging makes a magnetic battery pack hot, and heat makes phones slow their charging down. Anker’s fix in the MagGo 2 Pro is a tiny fan. The 10,000mAh pack charges at up to 25W over Qi2.2, and Anker says the fan keeps its back under about 97 degrees Fahrenheit while it works. Anker rates it to take an iPhone 17 Pro to 50 percent in about 25 minutes. A screen shows battery level and charging speed, a built-in stand props the phone up for in-flight movies, and the USB-C port refills the pack at 45W. It costs $109.99. Older phones, including the iPhone 15 Pro, top out at 15W.

Google hadn’t released a new standalone smart speaker since the Nest Audio in 2020. The Google Home Speaker is built around Gemini for Home instead of the old Assistant, so you can stack several requests into one sentence or correct yourself mid-command. It plays 360-degree sound from a 58mm driver, two of them pair with a Google TV Streamer for surround sound, and it doubles as a Thread border router and Matter hub. It costs $99.99 and includes six months of Google Home Premium, which adds Gemini Live and continued conversation. After the trial, Premium runs $10 per month.

A $20 smart plug makes a surprisingly good energy audit. The Shelly Plug Gen4 measures real-time power draw from whatever is plugged into it, so you can see how much that garage fridge or space heater actually pulls. It connects over Matter, Wi-Fi, or Zigbee, works with Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, SmartThings, and Home Assistant, and can run locally without touching the cloud. It handles loads up to 1,800 watts, with cutoffs for overheating, overcurrent, and voltage problems. Its built-in LED can change color to reflect current energy use. It costs $19.99 in black or white.

If you know someone constantly struggling to make work from the road work, the Sennheiser MOMENTUM 5 Wireless headphones are an audio oasis they will appreciate for years to come. The hybrid noise cancellation, 8-band graphic EQ, Snapdragon Sound, and other personalization features cut the noise and sculpt the sound, perfect for open-office escapees and in-control commuters. And a long-haul battery life delivers up to 57 hours of runtime, so playlists won’t run out somewhere over the Atlantic. Plus, the battery is user-replaceable, reducing e-waste and extending ownership. This is the perfect gift for music-loving control freqs.

Sonos isn’t the only way to fill a house with speakers that talk to each other. Denon’s redesigned Home lineup runs on HEOS, which can link up to 64 speakers across a home, and the three sizes scale with the room. The $399 Home 200 plays stereo from three tweeters and a 4-inch woofer. The $599 Home 400 adds two upward-firing drivers for Dolby Atmos Music, and the $799 Home 600 packs eight drivers, including dual 6.5-inch woofers, each with its own amplifier. All three take Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB-C, and aux. The stone and charcoal finishes look more like something from a furniture store than an electronics aisle.

The Bose LifeStyle Ultra Home Theater Set is perfect for homes that struggle with the volume of content and components. From the soundbar to the wireless satellites and subwoofer, everything is compact and design-conscious, perfect for a minimalist who doesn’t want to sacrifice expression. Bose SpeechClarity uses AI enhancement to make dialogue more audible without having to ride the volume constantly. CustomTune calibrates immersion to the room’s actual acoustics. And when it’s not movie night, stream music via AirPlay 2/Google Cast, no app required. Add more speakers later for a multiroom setup, making this a great gift for someone who wants to scale up a whole-home setup without sacrificing space.

39 products that will improve your everyday life.

Stan Horaczek is the executive gear editor at Popular Science. He oversees a team of gear-obsessed writers and editors dedicated to finding and featuring the newest, best, and most innovative gadgets on the market and beyond.

Tony Ware is the Managing Editor, Gear & Commerce for PopSci.com. #4741. The grossest thing you touch every day, according to science

Published Nov 1, 2026 5:02 PM EST

It’s probably not something you want to think about, but what do you think is the dirtiest thing you touch every day? If you commute via subway, you might suspect a stairwell handle or train pole as the most likely culprit. If you go from your house to your car to an office, maybe it’s the elevator button or the key fob you have to dig out of your bag. All very good guesses–you might even be tempted to pull out your phone and look up the correct answer.

“It might surprise people, but the dirtiest thing they encounter every day is their own cellphone,” says Caitlin Mangan, a Lab Manager for Gillson Sciences. “People take them everywhere with them, including the bathroom. They are touched thousands of times a day, without people cleaning them or washing their hands in between tasks.”

The University of Michigan’s Institute for Healthcare Policy & Innovation puts it this way: Your cellphone is 10 times dirtier than a toilet seat. Yeah, that’s pretty gross.

The frequency of contact contributes to that grossness. The study shows that, on average, people check their phones 47 times a day. And like your clothing and shoes, you carry your beloved phone through various environments of differing cleanliness levels. In fact, that subway pole may actually be cleaner than your iPhone.

“It depends on how often the areas are cleaned,” says Mangan. “For example, an office building door handle typically has less people touching it day-to-day, but because of that it might not be cleaned as frequently and therefore has a high risk of having germs. Whereas a subway pole that is cleaned daily and properly sanitized will have less germs to transfer.”

Cellphones have been known to carry skin bacteria like Staphylococcus and Streptococcus, as well as fecal bacteria like E. coli and Enterococcus faecalis. These bacteria can cause skin infections, strep throat, or gastrointestinal illnesses producing nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. You can help yourself by avoiding using your phone in the restroom, not placing it down on surfaces where germs likely lurk, and when speaking into it, not letting it touch your cheek or mouth.

Of course, you should also clean your phone with paper towels, alcohol, and cotton swabs whenever possible and follow the number one rule of germ spread prevention: Wash your hands frequently and thoroughly.

#4740. When Couples Grow Together

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

One of the most fulfilling experiences in any committed relationship is a couple growing together. However, growing together can feel vague and ambiguous, and at times even reduced to an achievement. Hopefully, this blog will offer concrete suggestions for growing together in ways that feel fulfilling and enjoyable. The idea that people come together and change along the way can feel intimidating. When couples grow together, change loses some of its uneasiness as they talk about it and encourage each other.

Couples can certainly grow together as they learn more about each other through shared activities. Playing tennis, painting the deck, ballroom dancing, scuba diving, and learning to play cribbage can add joy and connection. Shared hobbies do bring couples together. However, the depth of growing together mostly happens when couples focus their learning on one of three areas: Healing, Love, and Service.

Let’s look at each of these topics where deep learning can take place.

When each person’s healing becomes a learning priority, growing together can become the hallmark of the relationship, and the relationship can become an active container for personal growth.

When you want to learn more about healing, it’s important to remain compassionate as you self-examine. Another key is to remain curious without obsessing about every psychological nook and cranny.

Louise and John, a couple talking about growing together as they learn about healing. “John and I have overcome the challenges we faced as children and how those patterns can impact our marriage if we let them,” explained Louise.

“What a relief it has been to join Louise in her healing and getting over the idea that learning about healing is only for women. Also, I’m glad to have discovered a legacy of spousal betrayal, which I don’t want to reproduce and pass on to our children,” added John.

A deeply fulfilling place for couples to grow together is taking on an apprenticeship of love. That mostly means learning how to be more relational and emotionally intimate. It also means accepting that no one arrives able to give and receive love perfectly. We’re either devotionally participating in a love apprenticeship or not. Here are some concrete ways to participate.

Abigail and Cynthia talk about their apprenticeship to love as a couple.

“I’m noticing Abigail’s willingness to take more responsibility to love herself. What a gift that is for me, as I’m not primarily responsible for how she feels about herself. She tells me when she’s not feeling good about herself, and I ask what I can do. She says, 'Just listen.'"

“Blame seems to be on its way out of our relationship. Cynthia is committed to being more accountable. I decided to do it too. It is quite a joy to witness blame receding, with our individual maturation and the maturity of our relationship taking its place,” explained Abigail.

Growing together can involve quite a bit of psychology. Rather than getting hung up on stereotypical understandings of the word psychology, let the old original definition of the word guide you. In ancient Greek, psychology means “care of the soul.” Why not consider caring for the soul of your relationship?

#4739. Why Cancer Biomarker Testing Is Personal for Mark-Paul Gosselaar

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.

Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.

“Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline. “We are constantly aware of new technologies.”

Having seen people in his life navigate cancer diagnoses, Gosselaar is now raising awareness about the role of biomarker testing in cancer treatment through his partnership with AstraZeneca and its Meet Your Mark campaign.

The campaign aims to educate people facing cancer diagnoses and their loved ones about how biomarker testing may help doctors make more informed, personalized treatment decisions. It also encourages patients to discuss testing with their healthcare teams.

“Biomarkers may tell doctors the specific type of cancer present and if targeted therapies or immunotherapy might help,” Mark Socinski, MD, oncologist and Executive Medical Director of the AdventHealth Cancer Institute, told Healthline.

He explained that biomarkers are typically genes or proteins that doctors measure through blood or tissue tests. They are used to help guide treatment in numerous diseases but are especially powerful tools in many types of cancer.

“They help decode why cancers behave differently, even when two people have the same cancer type,” said Socinski. “However, while biomarker testing provides useful information, it does not guarantee a specific outcome.”

Despite those limitations, Socinski sees promise in the shift from one-size-fits-all cancer treatment to care tailored to each patient’s specific cancer characteristics.

“Biomarker testing does play a critical role here, and it is important for people to be aware of the potential benefits,” Socinski said. “It may help change the course of a person’s treatment journey.”

Gosselaar hopes that greater awareness of biomarker testing can help people facing a cancer diagnosis feel more informed about their treatment options.

“A lot of the time, when a loved one or someone who has been diagnosed with cancer [it can] feel like your world is in a tailspin,” he said. “I wanted to get the word out for anyone who’s going through a cancer diagnosis, or a caretaker, to know that biomarker testing is an option, because even though two cancers are similar, their tumors can act very differently and biomarker testing may help the medical expert with more personalized treatment.”

As part of the campaign, Gosselaar took part in a commercial, something he hadn’t done since before his days on “Saved by the Bell.”

“This was the first time that I actually had to be on set and not be a character; I had to be me talking about this very serious issue,” he said.

While it was a challenging experience, he said it was also fulfilling.

“I enjoyed the process, and to be able to use my platform to be able to spread the word; it means a lot to me,” he said. “I’m very selective of the things that I want to attach myself to, and this seemed like the right fit.”

He particularly enjoyed recreating Zack Morris’s signature “timeout” gesture from “Saved by the Bell,” which allowed his character to freeze time and speak directly to the camera.

“Using something from the past that was such a symbolic gesture to so many people of my generation that are now my age and possibly going through [cancer] or knowing someone who’s going through [cancer to] direct them to [this campaign], means a lot,” he said.

Beyond his efforts to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing, Gosselaar is equally focused on taking care of his own health.

Getting quality sleep is one of his top priorities. He sleeps on a high-tech mattress that monitors sleep stages, heart rate, heart rate variability, and respiratory rate. He also uses a biometric health and fitness tracker, prioritizes healthy eating, and uses saunas and red light therapy.

“We do everything that we possibly can, but I’m less about longevity and more about just living a healthy lifestyle,” Gosselaar said. “I want to continue doing the things that I’ve done since I was a child…without feeling held back by my health.”

As he embraces his 50s, he said he’d like to live a long life for his children and future grandchildren. He started taking his health seriously in his 40s after undergoing shoulder surgery.

“[It] really made me realize [that] all the damage I had done in my 20s and 30s sort of adds up later in life, and that’s probably something that I would tell the younger me… to preserve a little bit more and take [an] approach that recovery is just as important as the workout because I did not use my recovery very well; it was not a priority for me,” said Gosselaar.

He also makes time for himself every day. He said doing so makes him a better person and more able to care for his wife and four children.

“[It’s] something that I believe in; that I need to do something for myself before I can do something for someone else. Or if I do something for someone else, then I have to equalize that by doing something for me,” he said.

Daily physical activity also helps support his mental well-being.

“I need to do something where I challenge myself, and it could be as simple as a walk. It could be as simple as just getting outside and lifting something heavy [or] taking bags of groceries and taking the long way into your house,” Gosselaar said.

“Like challenging yourself with picking up things, you know, taking backpacks from the car from your kids and seeing if you can carry three in one hand…or going into the gym and spending an hour in the gym, or 30 minutes, or just moving.”

When he’s in the sauna, he works on breathing and clearing his thoughts.

“Some people need to meditate, some people need to talk to somebody. I encourage all of that because I think all of that helps,” he said.

“I’ve done them all. I’ve done the cold plunging, I’ve done all that stuff…some of it works, and some of it doesn’t; it’s whatever you believe in. So I just encourage people to stay healthy and move, get outside, and help other people.”

#4738. How Europe’s battery passport could have a big impact on US e-bikes

Europe is preparing to introduce a new requirement that could change how electric bicycle batteries are tracked, repaired, recycled, and potentially even resold. Starting in February 2027, new e-bike batteries sold in the European Union will be required to carry a digital battery passport, giving each battery its own digital identity and making important information about its origins and characteristics accessible throughout its lifetime.

And while the rules are European, their impact could eventually reach American e-bike riders, too.

The battery passport requirement comes from the EU’s 2023 Batteries Regulation, which established new standards for battery sustainability, traceability, and transparency. The rules cover several categories of batteries, including those used in electric cars, electric bicycles, electric scooters, and other light electric vehicles.

Beginning February 18, 2027, newly placed batteries in these categories will need digital passports accessible through QR codes. Scanning the code will provide access to information about the battery, though exactly what users can see will depend on their authorization level.

The information can include details such as the battery’s manufacturer, chemistry, capacity, cycle count, carbon footprint, and materials used in its construction. The system also provides for information about battery performance and durability, including data related to battery health and degradation.

That last part could be particularly interesting for electric bicycle owners.

Anyone who has purchased a used electric bicycle knows that the battery is often one of the biggest unknowns. A bike might look nearly new, but its battery could have hundreds of charge cycles under its belt and significantly reduced capacity.

Even a quick test ride before a secondhand e-bike purchase may fail to demonstrate just how little capacity remains in a heavily used battery.

With replacement e-bike batteries costing hundreds of dollars, that’s a pretty important detail.

The battery passport system could eventually help address that problem by making battery information more transparent. However, there’s an important distinction: the regulations don’t necessarily guarantee that everyday consumers will be able to scan a QR code and immediately see a battery’s remaining health percentage. Some of that information may be restricted to authorized users.

Even so, the system could help repair shops, recyclers, and secondhand buyers better understand the batteries they’re dealing with.

It could also make life more complicated for e-bike manufacturers, especially smaller brands that will now need to ensure their batteries meet the new documentation and traceability requirements.

There’s currently no equivalent nationwide battery passport requirement for electric bicycles in the United States, but that doesn’t mean American riders won’t eventually benefit.

I think it's really great that European consumer protection laws have a global impact because of the size of the European single market, and that they make life just a little bit easier for consumers all over the world. USB-C was just the beginning—there's more to come!

Many major e-bike manufacturers sell their products in both Europe and North America. US-based companies like Trek and Specialized have major markets in Europe, and will have to comply with the new law. Chinese companies and other Asian manufacturers will also need to produce compliant batteries. Once those companies have developed systems to track individual batteries and provide digital passports for their European products, they may find it easier to extend those systems to their American models rather than maintain entirely separate processes.

That doesn’t mean US-bound batteries will automatically receive passports, but it could create an interesting spillover effect.

And considering how expensive e-bike batteries can be, anything that makes it easier to understand their condition, verify their origins, or facilitate repairs could be a welcome development.

For now, Europe is leading the charge on battery transparency. But if the system proves useful, American e-bike riders might eventually get some of the same benefits without waiting for Washington to catch up.

#4737. Bald eagle mistaken for trashbag on the road to recovery

Published Nov 2, 2026 9:00 AM EST

A Pennsylvania resident recently arrived home to find what looked like an unassuming black trash bag in their yard. But the bag moved and lifted its head. Turns out, it was not a bag, but a bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus). And something was very wrong with her.

A state Game Warden brought the eagle to Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in southern Pennsylvania to be checked out. The bird couldn’t stand and her legs were limp, which is a typical symptom of spinal trauma. Nonetheless, the team also tested the eagle for lead poisoning, and found that she indeed had lead in her system. Even though the eagle wasn’t showing signs of such poisoning, they weren’t surprised by these results.

In a 2022 study published in the journal Science, researchers investigated lead exposure in 1,210 bald and golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) in North America and found chronic lead poisoning in 46 to 47 percent of both eagles and acute lead poisoning in 27 to 33 percent of bald eagles. Lead exposure in eagles and other avian scavengers mostly occurs when they consume the remains of animals shot with lead ammunition and left behind by hunters.

“Lead poisoning is so common that even eagles brought in for other injuries are now routinely tested for it, and almost all show some level of lead in their system,” Tracie Young, Raven Ridge Wildlife Center director, tells Popular Science.

Even small quantities of lead can be extremely toxic. Lead poisoning can cause brain swelling, trouble breathing, weak muscles, dehydration, starvation, kidney and liver problems, or seizures, Young explains.

“Nerve damage can cause them to lose vision, coordination, and normal movement, so the bird may look ‘drunk’ or not be able to stand,” she continues. “When these eagles are starving, they lose their hunting skills and can’t catch food. As scavengers, they look for roadkill, but because they are uncoordinated, they often get hit by vehicles.”

It’s likely that this is what happened to the trash-bag-looking female eagle in Pennsylvania. At the wildlife center, she received chelation therapy for the lead poisoning. Chelation therapy involves the administration of administering specialized chemical agents that attach to the lead molecules in the bird’s blood and form a compound that is expelled, mostly via urine. The eagle also received physical therapy to regain strength in her legs and mitigate spinal pain and swelling.

Her rehabilitation process has been challenging, but not without its rewards. She is currently able to stand and lives in an outdoor area with an open space where she can continue her rehabilitation process. The eagle is a good candidate for release, but Young says she will require weeks of flight training.

“We urge all hunters and anglers to make a crucial choice: opt for lead-free ammunition and lead-free fishing gear,” the wildlife center wrote in a Facebook post. “This single decision at checkout can significantly improve the lives of countless eagles and other wildlife suffering from lead poisoning.”

#4736. What Every Parent Should Know About Campus Sexual Assault

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 6, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

Campus sexual assault has been in the news lately due to the sexual assault allegations at Cornell. Sexual assault has always been a fear of many parents as they send their daughters to college. While both women and men can be sexually assaulted, the victims are predominantly women, which will be the focus of this article.

Reports show 26% of college women experience sexual assault at some point in their college years. While most men do not assault women, surveys showed that the percentage of college men who admitted to behavior that met the definition of rape or attempted rape increased from 8% in 1985 to 13% in 2015. Of note, rape is a term that means nonconsensual penetrative sex, while sexual assault includes any nonconsensual sexual contact.

Parents should be aware of the nature and frequency of sexual assault on campus so they can talk about prevention. They can let their children know they will support them if the worst happens.

Over my 30-year career as a psychiatrist, I have worked with hundreds of college students who have been assaulted. I will share stories I have heard to offer insights about this experience and what helps students cope. I will also discuss sexual assault prevention programs.

Here are statements I have heard over the years.

“I didn’t tell anyone about it for a week because I felt like it was my fault. I should not have had so much to drink. But I told him no and pushed back, and he still went ahead. He is in my friend group. I thought no one would believe me. Then, as I looked back on what happened, I realized he raped me. Now I keep replaying it in my head and can't fall asleep."

“The campus victim advocate referred me to you as I’ve been feeling depressed since I was raped and I think I need medication. And I’m not sure what to do. I did a rape kit after the assault, but I don't know if I want to go ahead and press charges. From what I hear, most cases don’t even get prosecuted.”

These examples highlight certain aspects of sexual assault.

Parents have an important role in educating their daughters about the prevention of sexual assault. They can encourage their children to do the following:

Step up and intervene or call police if they witness dangerous sexual situations. There is evidence that bystander education can reduce violence towards women on campus, and more campuses are offering bystander training programs.

Let your daughter know that if she is ever assaulted, you will be there for her as a safe space and sounding board. Follow her lead as she decides if she wants to contact the school or law enforcement. Encourage her to take the following actions.

During my psychiatry career, I have witnessed women who experience sexual assault resiliently move forward with their lives. A strong support system of friends and family will promote their recovery. Parents can maintain an open dialogue with their children about sexual safety on campus and encourage colleges to implement programs to end campus sexual violence.

#4734. GLP-1s May Help Lower Diabetes, Heart Risks Better Than Standard Prevention

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a new study.

Researchers said GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.

They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

The researchers noted that GLP-1 users also had a lower risk of death from any cause as well as fewer heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure events compared with metformin users.

“The great news with prediabetes is that it’s still possible to reverse the progression of the disease,” said Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, MD, a study author and research fellow in cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, in a press release. “This research may add to the case for considering GLP-1 medications earlier for certain patients, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes.”

Serra noted that metformin still remains an effective treatment for people with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

“This is less about replacing one medication with another and more about discussing additional options with specific patients,” he said.

The researchers presented their findings at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

David Cutler, MD, a family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the findings were “quite impressive.”

“It elevates the comfort of prescribing GLP-1 drugs as a front-line treatment,” he told Healthline.

Robert Eckel, MD, a former president of the American Heart Association who was likewise not involved in the study, agrees the research provides more options for patients and prescribers.

“GLP-1s provide another option for prevention, perhaps as an add-on therapy. However, costs and access to these medications are important factors,” said Eckel, an endocrinologist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, in the press release.

For their study, the researchers analyzed the medical records of 256,000 adults in the United States with prediabetes and obesity. About 76% of the subjects were women, and the average age of the participants was 52.

About half of those studied were taking GLP-1 drugs with the active ingredient semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide.

The other half had been prescribed metformin, a medication used to help manage blood sugar levels in adults and some children with type 2 diabetes by decreasing glucose production in the liver, reducing glucose absorption from food, and improving the body’s insulin sensitivity.

The researchers reported that the people in the study who were taking GLP-1 drugs had a 1.5 times higher chance of reversing high blood sugar to healthy levels compared to people who were using metformin.

The researchers also noted that GLP-1 medication users had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death from any cause.

They added that GLP-1 medications were associated with 15% fewer heart attacks, 20% fewer strokes, 25% fewer cases of heart failure, and 8% fewer cases of atrial fibrillation (AFib), a common type of irregular heartbeat.

The researchers cautioned that their study is observational and, therefore, cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship. They also noted they relied on prescription records, so the frequency and dosage at which patients took their medication was not reflected.

In addition, the GLP-1 drugs were grouped together, so individual differences between medications were not considered.

Eckel said in the news release that the benefits for people taking GLP-1 drugs were probably mainly due to weight loss. Eckel noted that the research results open up a wide range of possibilities.

“This is an important finding because the GLP-1 receptor agonists are commonly used today and this is a population that in the transition from prediabetes to diabetes are at increasing risk for cardiovascular disease,” Eckel said in a taped interview alongside the study findings.

Cutler pointed out that several GLP-1 drugs also target blood sugar levels and insulin production. They could be effective in people with prediabetes who don’t have weight management issues.

Cutler noted that these people, however, might be reluctant to take GLP-1 drugs because they may not be experiencing symptoms of their prediabetes but could develop side effects with the medications.

“They would not be getting any immediate benefits,” Cutler said. He added that metformin, which was first used clinically in 1958, remains an effective alternative. “It’s been proven safe, effective, and it’s very cheap,” Cutler said.

It’s estimated that 40 million people in the United States have diabetes, with more than 90% of those cases being type 2 diabetes, a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose levels that results from the body’s ineffective response to insulin or insufficient insulin production.

It’s also estimated that 115 million adults in the United States have prediabetes, a condition in which a person has higher-than-normal blood sugar levels but not high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes.

Around 5–10% of people with prediabetes develop diabetes every year. More broadly, up to 70% of people with prediabetes eventually develop diabetes.

Medication is sometimes prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. Lifestyle changes can help reverse type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, as well as prevent the progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

Cutler said the lifestyle changes needed to prevent type 2 diabetes are pretty clear.

“The most important thing for people with prediabetes to know is they should lose weight, reduce their carbs, exercise daily and, if that doesn’t work, then consider medication,” he said.
